speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. C. W. G. GIBSON (Minister of National Revenue):
subtopic: EXTENSION OF FILING DATE FOR T2 QUESTIONNAIRE IN RESPECT OF 1942 CORPORATE RETURN
speechtext:
On June 15 the hon.
member for Cumberland (Mr. Black) asked whether the time would be extended for the filing of income tax returns for 1942, pointing out that chartered accountants and business firms would find it almost impossible to file their returns by the prescribed date. I said that at that time no change was contemplated; but I should now like to announce that to-day a notice is being sent out to all inspectors of income tax, as follows:
You may advise the public in general that there will be no extension in the time of filing the required individual and corporate income
tax returns which are due on 30th June. This does not apply to the information return known as T2 questionnaire which has been introduced for the first time this year and requires considerable care and attention in its preparation. Inasmuch as it is supplementary to the T2 corporate return this is to advise that penalties will not be imposed in respect to the fiscal year ending 31st December, 1942, if the T2 questionnaire is lodged on or before 31st July, 1943, provided that the T2 questionnaire is signed not only by the required officials of the company but also accompanied by the auditor's supporting certificate, without which the time is not extended. No extension will be granted for the filing of T2 questionnaire in respect of fiscal periods ending after 31st December, 1942.
A considerable amount of work is entailed in the preparing and certifying of this questionnaire, and it is considered that by extending the time for filing it, considerable relief will be afforded.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF FILING DATE FOR T2 QUESTIONNAIRE IN RESPECT OF 1942 CORPORATE RETURN
speechtext: Of course that is another question. The questionnaire is another document.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF FILING DATE FOR T2 QUESTIONNAIRE IN RESPECT OF 1942 CORPORATE RETURN
speechtext: No, it has to be filed with the return.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF FILING DATE FOR T2 QUESTIONNAIRE IN RESPECT OF 1942 CORPORATE RETURN
speechtext: It has to be filed with the corporate return; but I thought that in the other case referred to the minister was giving consideration to an extension.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF FILING DATE FOR T2 QUESTIONNAIRE IN RESPECT OF 1942 CORPORATE RETURN
speechtext: The T2 questionnaire is filed in conjunction with the T2 form, and I understand after consultation with the accountants that it is the T2 questionnaire which has been holding them up, because it requires so much care in preparation, and must be certified by the accountant.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF FILING DATE FOR T2 QUESTIONNAIRE IN RESPECT OF 1942 CORPORATE RETURN
speechtext: Did I understand the minister to say that firms whose fiscal year ends later than December 31, 1942, would of necessity have to file form T2 questionnaire before June 30?

subtopic: EXTENSION OF FILING DATE FOR T2 QUESTIONNAIRE IN RESPECT OF 1942 CORPORATE RETURN
speechtext: No, they do not file this until six months after the close of the business year, so that they would not be filing it by June 30, in any case.

["As I shall not be able to read this in ten minutes I shall leave it for another time. The hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) asked if the publication Wings pays for itself. It does not. The monthly revenue more than covers the purchase of materials and the typesetting that is done by a civilian firm. In effect, the only public expense is for salaries of service personnel and for the shipping of the paper to the stations. It is still a new venture and has every right to expect that, as it develops, expenditures will be reduced. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle asked about the cost of publishing Wings. The total cost is $1,487 a month. The revenue for the first three months was $540 a month. The monthly deficit is $947 at the present time. The cost is made up of $346 for materials; $112 for typesetting; $265 for shipping; and $764 for editorial staff; or a total of $1,487.
The hon. member for St. John-Albert (Mr. Hazen) asked if buses are attached to the
Pennfield Ridge station to take personnel to the city. Buses are not attached to this station to take personnel to the city. Saint John is thirty-nine miles from the station, and a civilian bus service is in operation. He asked also if orders have been issued to restrict the use of staff cars. The answer is, yes. The King's Regulations and Orders for the Royal Canadian Air Force, Canadian air publication No. 23, gives specific instructions with regard to restricting the use of staff cars. Orders are issued periodically with regard to this procedure.
The hon. member for Prince Edward-Lennox (Mr. Tustin) inquired about the cost of posters. One hundred and fifty thousand posters, size twenty-five by thirty-eight inches, were produced at a cost of $25,302, or, roughly, seventeen cents each. Twenty thousand posters in French were produced at a cost of $6,000. Fifty thousand posters in connection with recruiting for the women's division were produced at a cost of $6,900, or, roughly, fourteen cents each.
The hon. member for Peterborough West (Mr. Fraser) asked whether helicopters can land on water. They can be fitted with flotation bags which will permit them to be so landed.
The hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson) asked if the Jacobs engine has been satisfactory. Since the original teething troubles were overcome, the Jacobs engine has given good satisfaction. A recent survey has shown that accidents on account of engine failure in aircraft fitted with Jacobs engines occur at a rate of only one in about twenty-nine thousand hours of flying, a rate which compares favourably with other engines. I think these are all the questions I can answer before eleven o'clock.
Progress reported."]

Under this particular item there are a number of questions I desire to ask, some of which I asked the other day, which so far the minister has not answered. In the statement respecting production of aircraft the minister said the number produced to date is approximately 8,000 planes. I should like to ask him whether the
8,000	planes represent actual production in Canada, except for engines, or whether it includes importations from the United States. On November 14, 1941, the minister gave a statement with regard to the production of planes in this country, and as reported at page 4082 of Hansard, he said:
Our aircraft industry has manufactured in Canada and placed in service since the outbreak of war, or has assembled in Canada, 3,749 aircraft. In addition, we have received from the United States in the same period 1,268 aircraft. The present average rate of production is approximately forty per week for all types, and in this regard it should be pointed out that the present production includes a heavier proportion of advanced trainers and service aircraft than in the earlier months of production.
The other day when I asked the minister why there was a reduction per month in the number of planes being produced, he replied that of course the poundage was very much greater. What has it been each year since 1940? When I look back over the Hansards that I have here, since the outbreak of the war, and read the statements made by the minister at each successive sitting of the house, wherein with pride he pointed to the production of aircraft in Canada and the anticipated increase in production, the statement is so much like the statement he made the other day that I feel justified in asking him now to give the Canadian people the
picture with regard to aircraft production, not in generalities but in particulars, so that people will be able to understand whether or not aircraft production in Canada is in keeping with munitions production and the like. I therefore ask him to give particulars of the different types of planes that have been produced. How many Ansons have been produced since May 14, 1942, at which time the minister stated in the house that production was over 600 planes? Furthermore the minister said-

Let us have one question at a time. My memory -perhaps is not as good as my hon. friend's, and he has notes while I have not.
' Mr. DIEFENBAKER: The minister's memory should be fairly good, because that is one question which significantly he has not answered in the past.
The hon. member wishes to know how many Ansons Canada has produced,
How is that number of 8,000 planes made up? How many Ansons are there and how many of various other types?
As to the number of Ansons, Canada had produced as at the end of May last, 1,850.

What about the
other types of planes?
What type does the hon. member want to know about?
The types included in the 8,000 planes which the minister says have been produced in Canada.

I shall be glad to put them on Hansard if my hon. friend wishes. I have never done this before and I think it is breaking the security rules. However, he has asked for it and he can take the responsibility for the answer.
Oh, no.
Certainly he will.
That answer is not fair.
Why not?

The people of Canada want to know whether or not the flowery statements with respect to production are justified by the facts. If the minister says-and this has always been my attitude-that in the public interest, for security reasons, he cannot furnish this information, then I ask him how it is that information as to production in various types is furnished by others outside of parliament.
War Appropriation-Supplies

My hon. friend says that the people demand to know, and he is a tribune of the people, and therefore I am certainly going to tell him. If I get into trouble, for security reasons, my hon. friend must share the responsibility.
In the field of elementary trainers Canada has built 1,384 Tiger Moths; 10 Menasco Moths; 126 Wireless Moths; 409 Cornell trainers; 431 Fleet 16 trainers, making a total of planes built in the field of elementary trainers of 2,360.
In the field of advanced trainers Canada has built 1,059 Harvards; 51 Norsemen; 101 Fleet 60's; 367 Bolingbrokes; 1,850 Ansons, and 150 Lysanders, making a total in the field of advanced trainers of 3,578.
In the field of service aircraft Canada has built 15 Sharks; 15 Grummonds; 32 Stran-raers; 8 Deltas; 75 Lysanders; 69 Norsemen; 169 Bolingbrokes; 63 PBY boats; 1,451 Hurricanes; 160 Hampdens, and 19 Mosquitos. Those figures are up to the end of May. The figure I gave the other day, of 21 Mosquitos, was up to date.

Nineteen
Mosquitos?
To the end of May. That makes a total of 2,076 service aircraft, and a grand total of aeroplanes built up to the end of May of 8,014.
When was the contract for the Mosquitos let with the de Havilland company on which we had a production of nineteen planes?
I have not the exact date.
Was it not placed in the fall of 1941?
The first negotiations were opened in September, 1941.
I understand that the contract for the Mosquitos was placed with the de Havilland company late in the fall of 1941, the negotiations having preceded the letting of the contract.
Placed by whom?
I did not say by whom.
Who placed the contract?
I suppose it is the Department of Munitions and Supply. And the production on that contract has been nineteen Mosquitos.
Nineteen to the end of May. Let us be accurate at least.

To the end of May. I am quite glad to take the minister's statement. I have been prompted to make this statement because I hold in my hand an article from a weekly journal, dated the 19th of June, entitled "Hatching Mosquitos", and the statements contained in this article are in a degree a reflection on the minister's department and on the production of Mosquitos. The article gives a pretty lurid description of what has happened, I do not vouch for the truth of it, but it is being broadcast throughout the country, and if it is not true the matter ought to be cleared up. If it is true there ought to be an admission on the record. The article starts off by making a declaratory statement:
. Canada's war-time production is the biggest in the world-for its size. The way tanks, guns, planes and all other munitions of war are turned out by the publicity branch of the Department of Munitions and Supply would astonish even the Russians.

What is my hon. friend
reading from?
I will show it to my hon. friend when I am through.
Tell me; I am entitled to know.
It is an article by Dennis Pratt in the News.
What News?
Perhaps the minister-

In other words, Judith
Robinson.
I do not care who it is.
I am entitled to know.
I said' I would hand the article over to the minister when I am through reading it.
Put it on Hansard.

It goes on to say:
A ease in point is the production of Mosquito bombers by the de Havilland Company of Canada. The contract for these planes was placed in the fall of 1941, and almost immediately the publicity branch of Munitions and Supply went into action. It had bombers "in production" at the plant in no time, and then turned its attention to other supplies which needed boosting.
But the actual machines at the plant, having got into production, stayed there and never came out.

War Appropriation-Supplies
Now we have the admission from the minister that in two and a half years only nineteen planes have been produced on this contract up to the end of May.
Exactly how does my hon. friend arrive at two and a half years?
From the fall of 1941 to the fall of 1942 is one year, and now it is the summer of 1943. That is in excess of two and a half years.
One and a half years.

Just under two years-my error. I am not like the minister when I find I am in error I am glad to say that I am mistaken, but the Minister of Munitions and Supply, like most of the members on the treasury benches, never admits an error. I will admit that there is one great exception, and that is the Minister of National Defence for Air. By his very humility and his candor he inspires confidence, which the Minister of Munitions and Supply does not inspire.
Ohl

All right; I hear the jeers from across the line, but I am not impressed by them. It would be far better if we could have a little more candor about these things from the treasury benches, and say we made a mistake.

Let us be careful. The hon. member for Lake Centre challenged my statement on the number of planes produced, and I have given him the production by chapter and verse. Just what is my hon. friend blustering about now? It is all very well to bluster, but it is just as well to keep your feet on the ground.
I do not usually bluster.
You bluster a great deal.

I am not blustering. What I say is this: all down through the years because of the puffing and publicity by the department's publicity branch the Canadian people have been led to believe that production was enormous, immense.
It is.

The publicity was always in advance of the production. I think I realize some of the reasons why the production did not come up to expectations; there must have been many bottlenecks, many difficulties encountered by the minister. I
think it would be much better for him to be frank and say: We hoped to do thus and so, but for reasons unforeseen we could not do it. That is what I suggest to the minister.

I did not say that we have done thus and so except in the report I made to parliament, and if my hon. friend can successfully challenge any statement in the report I made to parliament I shall be very glad to have him do so now. Otherwise I think we might very well suspend this attack.

All right;
I am used to taking lectures from across the line, and it does not bother me a bit. I would like the minister to read this article.
I am particular about what I read. That is not one of my favourite authors

I see; the minister never wants to learn. I suggest to him that he would be wise to study the criticisms that are made of his department; it might bring constructive and productive results. When I was leader of the opposition I always felt that constructive criticism in newspapers not only had a chastening effect upon my soul but it did me good, and I should think the same thing would apply to the minister. As I said before, the trouble with the minister is that he never admits error, and I suggest that is a weakness. That is why the public have not the confidence they should have had in some of the statements that have been made by the minister's publicity department in the past. The whole history of the Moth contract and the production under that contract is confusing. I do not understand why production has not been greater, and the minister should make that clear. I am not going to blame the minister personally; I think he is just as desirous of seeing production come off the assembly lines of the de Havilland plant as I am.
Far more so.

Maybe.
I do not know where that came from-
It oame right from here, and I meant it.

I would expect anything from a back bencher over there. But approaching this matter in the calm light of mild philosophy, if I may use that term, I suggest to the minister that in his statements as to production he should confine himself to what has been done and not give us so much about what is going to be done. That is the point.

War Appropriation-Supplies

When have I given the hon. member anything about what is going to be done? Since my hon. friend has given me his expert opinion, perhaps I might give him the expert opinion of Mr. Butler, the chairman of the board of the de Havilland company in England. I quote from a cable recently received from our London office about Mosquito production:
While Butler admits inevitable mistakes in estimates he states that rate of Canadian production to-day is good and stresses that it compares more than favourably with early production in each of the two factories here.
The statement is that Mosquito production is good?
Yes.
What is the date of that?

Since we are discussing the production of aeroplanes perhaps this would be a good place to ask the minister a couple of questions following the discussion we had yesterday. The minister said he would be glad to tell the house the price per pound of sheet aluminum, and I should like to have that in order to get the record straight. Then I said to the minister yesterday at page 3828 of Hansard:
As I understand it the base price is fifteen cents a pound, Canadian funds, and that to-day we are paying twenty and a half cents a pound.
Mr. Howe: That is right, except that fifteen cents is United States funds.
That is right.
I did not understand that yesterday. The base price in Canadian funds is 16 cents?
Yes.
Not 16J cents?

No. There are certain adjustments. These prices all have delivery points. The 15 cents in American funds is the base,, and to arrive at the Canadian price, adjustments were made against our delivery point as compared to the United States delivery point, and the two represent equal prices, all things being taken into consideration. The actual price came out at sixteen and a very small fraction, and it was made sixteen flat.
And is the 5i cents in Canadian or United States funds?
It is in Canadian funds.
So the last adjustment gave us a price of 21J cents a pound for the aluminum, 16 plus 5J?
That is right.
That is for the ingots?
Yes.

What is the price per
pound of sheet aluminum, which is required by the companies who are making aeroplanes and so on?

The price of aluminum sheet of common gauge, which means the standard alloy-these sheets are an alloy of aluminum -is 25 cents; that is the base price, with extras up to 35 cents for extra gauges. My hon. friend knows how sheet metal is sold. The base price is 25 cents, and the prices for common gauge run up to 35 cents; there is a long price list.
Is that per pound?

Yes. I do not know just
what is put in the alloys; and perhaps my hon. friend is not interested in this price, but for the strong alloy the base price is 35 cents and for certain gauges it runs up to 50 cents a pound. For the rods, common gauge, which compare with the common gauge sheets, the base price is the same, 25 cents running up to 35 cents for odd sizes. For the strong alloy in the rods, the price runs from 35 cents to 50 cents.

These are the base
prices?
These are the actual prices.
The base price is from 25 cents to 35 cents?
Twenty-five cents. Always in sheet metal there is a certain gauge which is considered the base price, and gauges above and below that have higher prices, due to mechanical differences.

Can the minister tell
the committee what percentage of duralumin is used in a modem fighting plane? I understand that the greater part of the metal used is this hard, high tension alloy.

It varies greatly as between
planes, as my hon. friend will easily understand. We would need to know the particular plane in question, and check back on it.

Take a Hurricane, for
instance.

War Appropriation-Supplies

That plane weighs about
seven thousand pounds, and the duralumin probably would amount to about 25 per cent of the weight of the plane. That is as near as I can give it to my hon. friend.
Can the minister tell us whether the number of Ansons he mentioned includes those which were shipped to Canada from England and assembled here?

No, there were 1,900 Ansons
that came from England, which were assembled here, and those were entirely outside the figures I gave my hon. friend.

Then there were 1,850
produced here and 1,900 shipped and assembled here?
Yes.

Did any part of
the 8,000 planes represent parts manufactured in the United States, brought to Canada and assembled here into planes?

No; the only part brought
in from the United States was the engine.

I have one or two general questions I should like to put to the minister. Last night there was some discussion as to the duty of a member of parliament in connection with the various war plants under the control of the minister. I was chairman of the Toronto harbour commission when the plant referred to last night by hon. gentlemen to my left was brought to the city of Toronto in the last war. Since this war began I have taken it to be my duty not to enter a war plant unless I was invited, and I have never received an invitation. One reason has been that since the war began we were supposed to have an honourable agreement among ourselves, as members of the House of Commons, to conduct our affairs during the war without regard to political considerations at all, in order to attain an all-out war effort in this country following the practice that has been adopted and so well carried out in the old country. There the labour unions agreed with the government that there would be no more peace ballots and no more general strikes until Hitler was beaten.
There are no labour unions under the axis powers; they were all abolished. There would be none in this country or on the continent of North America if we should lose this war. This is the most critical year of the whole war; and while I have in my constituency a great many people who work in these plants I have told them that I do not think it is my duty to interfere as to the merits of rival
unions, since the onus is upon the government of the day to decide all matters in regard to labour conditions and the conduct of this war. I can tell you, however, that those who are serving in the armed forces, especially in the citizens' army, are doing more work twenty-four hours a day for $1.30 than many people working in our factories at much higher wages. I see these men in uniform on the trains; I know thousands and tens of thousands of them in the three services and I can tell you that the people at the front and those in the services in this country are wondering what we are doing over here, why we are meddling and interfering as we are in war plants and strikes. I have no objection to the stand taken by hon. members to my left; it is their privilege. But they are not the only labour party in the House of Commons. Hon. members in this part of the house have taken the stand that we should not use the war to advance our party. In fact I had not been in a munitions plant since the war started until last Friday, when for about half an hour I visited the de Havilland plant. With the two labour unions contending for mastery in this country, it is the duty of the government to step in with a strong national win-the^war labour policy. The onus is upon the government and it is the government's function, so long as it is in office to see that the war work is carried on and that the war is paramount until Hitler is beaten.
May I say a few words regarding the fifty-mile bus rule. I hope this absurd regulation will be abolished by the minister as soon as possible, because it reacts unfavourably against the troops and their families in various parts of the country. And I can say this further, regarding housing, that if we wait for the government to supply houses in Toronto, both for war workers and the civilian population, we will wait until doomsday. If the government would remove the restraint from private builders, and back them with government finance, with moneys under the housing act obtained through the banks, there would be plenty of houses around the Toronto district, especially houses of the smaller type. If the government would see fit to adopt a forward policy' on such a scheme by obtaining money from the banks in the usual way, and thereby help builders to obtain more materials, the situation would be far better both now and after the war.
I believe coal is more or less under the control of the Minister of Munitions and Supply. The shortage is to a great extent a question of transportation and delivery. Is it or is it not true that the municipalities have been promised that they will get their supplies of coal? One of the most dangerous men on
War Appropriation-Supplies

the north American continent is "General" John L. Lewis. I have read the speeches on May 1, May 7 and other dates and heard the radio addresses of that very able man who is President of the United States. I commend the strength of the President to the government of Canada. Let this government adopt some of the measures taken over there to defeat these trusts.
I have no complaint against the hon. member who brought up this question-far from it. In a great many ways I sympathize with labour in some war plants, and I have always been friendly to labour in the province from which I come. But I do say that when our troops overseas are fighting for $1.30 or $1.50 a day, it is not the time for us to have any division as to who shall have control in this plant, that plant or any other plant. We need a national labour policy in Canada, not only for the duration of the war, but when the war is over.
I do not wish to delay the passage of the minister's estimates. I do not know whether the Gallup poll applies to any of the industries over which he has control. But I can tell you that this Gallup poll, in the way it is being conducted throughout Canada, with all these galloping ghosts behind the scenes, is a real source of mischievous propaganda of all kinds for the prevention of the proper conduct of the war. It is political propaganda. The information is being given out by certain newspapers for purposes of political propaganda, and I wish to object to that practice. I hope the minister, his department and the government in general will have nothing to do with the Gallup poll, because it is all "Gallup" and no poll. No one knows who is behind it; no one knows who votes. I doubt if any ministers on the front benches have voted; I doubt if the leader of the opposition has a vote. I can tell you that this poll is no help to the war effort at all; it is a help to political propaganda, and to help some of those people in Canada who think that the empire should be allowed to go by default. This empire will never be allowed to go by default, and Canada is not going to be talked out of the British empire; Canada will have to be fought out of the British empire.

On an earlier occasion and again to-day the hon. member (Mr. Church) discussed the fifty-mile bus limit, but I do not believe an answer has been given by the minister. Perhaps the matter has been overlooked. The hon. member referred particularly to transportation of our armed forces. He has taken a vigorous stand with respect 
to this matter as it affects our fighting men.
I believe the minister might very well give the committee an answer.

The transit controller is '
responsible for transportation within communities, and transportation supplemental to communities, such as interurban bus lines. The hon. member knows that all our transportation is overloaded. Those responsible for allocating transportation facilities have undertaken-and I think successfully-to see that some means of transportation is available to every man who needs to travel. But in doing so they found it necessary to eliminate duplicate means of travel. In other words, if a man can travel by train to his destination, generally speaking he does not have the alternative of travelling by bus to the same destination. As all hon. members know, in general, cities served by railroads are also served by bus lines. For example, in pre-war days one could travel from Windsor to Toronto on either of two railway lines, and he could also travel by bus between those two cities. That was a desirable situation when we could afford to be lavish in our transportation facilities. However, when the war came along a problem developed, having to do with taking care of the short-haul passenger. I do not refer to the man who travelled from Windsor to Toronto, but rather to the man who wished to travel possibly from some country point between those two cities, to Windsor or to Toronto. With the congestion of travel, under the old system a bus would take a full load at Windsor, for Toronto, and would deliver that load in Toronto. That meant that the man living between the two cities was deprived of a necessary bus service, a service which is required to permit him to travel.
The fifty-mile rule was framed' to prevent the sort of travelling on buses I have described. It was aimed to prevent a bus from filling up at one terminal and moving to a terminal sixty or seventy miles away with a full load of passengers. The result of the fifty-mile service on the plan I have outlined is that passengers can take a bus at Toronto for any point between Toronto and some twenty miles east of Windsor. In other words, that area is served. Similarly, a man living more than twenty miles from Toronto can take a bus and travel to Windsor. But a man cannot take a bus in Toronto and travel on that bus to Windsor.
We have no objection to a man's travelling from Toronto to Windsor, but he can dd his travelling on either of two lines of railways. The fifty-mile rule has accomplished its

objective. We have been, able to provide a bus service for people to whom other forms of transportation are not available. It has not worked a hardship on the bus lines because there is plenty of travel of the type I mentioned to use the full capacity of the buses. It has not worked any hardship on the man desiring to travel from Toronto to Windsor. He knows very well that when he gets on the bus it will not take him to Windsor, and that he will have to get out when he has travelled fifty miles. Therefore that man travels by train. Now that the situation is understood I challenge anyone in this committee to tell me of a case of real hardship arising out of the fifty-mile rule.

I shall detain the committee but a short time, but I should like to refer briefly to what has been said by the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson). I see he is visiting on this side of the chamber. If he has had a change of heart and has come over here to support the government and the Minister of Munitions and Supply, perhaps it will not be necessary for me to say what I intended to say. However, assuming that he is going to return I shall continue. In his attack upon the Minister of Munitions and Supply he indicated that the minister was too much inclined to look to the future, to indicate what he hoped and what we all hoped this country would ultimately do in the matter of production. He said that instead of doing that, he ought to furnish more figures and records. He was challenged by the minister, who then paid no more attention to it-I think he was right-to give a single instance in which the minister had quoted figures which he had hoped to attain in the future but which had been wrong. I would commend to the hon. member for York-Sunbury the expression that there is always a far horizon for onward-looking men.
In many matters I have agreed with the hon. member, because I think during the last three years he has made some contributions to the discussion of the war effort. However, I believe if he had considered a little he would not have made the criticism he did. To the Minister of Munitions and Supply alone is due the magnificent Trans-Canada Air Lines which is going to play such a great part in the reconstruction of the nations of the world as soon as this war is over. It is easy to say that men look too much to the future, but I do not believe that that is the kind of criticism the people of Canada are seeking. They want men who have the vision to look into the future, men who are capable of converting this country as it has been converted
from peace time pursuits of turning out ploughshares into one of the greatest war production countries in the world.
For the benefit of the hon. member for York-Sunbury, if he is not content to take my statement, let me indicate what that grand little woman who addressed this house on June 16 said. She is reported on page 3721 of Hansard as follows:
. . . and the fact that per capita Canada has produced more for the war effort than any other member of the united nations are indicative of Canada's will to fight to victory.
That is the record we have among the nations of the world. Does my hon. friend dare to challenge her statement? If he is not content with that, let me remind him what Winston Churchill said on March 6 about Canada's war effort in production and in every other way. Mr. Churchill in a considered cable to the Prime Minister had this to say, as will be found on page 1023 of Hansard:
In the darkest days Canada, under your leadership, remained confident and true. Now the days are brighter, and w'hen victory is won, you will be able to look back with just pride upon a record surpassed by none.
Neither our Prime Minister nor our Minister of Munitions and Supply has attempted to take to himself personal credit for the war effort of Canada. They are both always careful to make it clear to the people that those responsible for the war effort which has produced the tributes of the kind I have just quoted are the men and women, the common people of Canada. There has never been any attempt to take unto the government the credit for the war effort of this country. ,1 should be the last to support a government which attempted to usurp the greater credit for the effort. The words of the hon. member are given heed to by the people of this country and it ill behooves him to attack the minister who more than any other-I am not trying to detract from what is due to or to make comparisons with the other hard-working ministers of the government-is responsible for the results of our war effort. It ill behooves a responsible member of this house to send out to the people of Canada that type of personal criticism. I should like to envision the kind of munitions and supply effort we would have had if the hon. member who has been the critic of to-day had been in charge of this department of government. The department and the minister deserve the greatest meed of praise and credit that the people of Canada can accord to them, aside altogether from any political credit or party spirit. I do hope the hon. member for York-Sunbury will not feel that I am putting it too strongly when I deprecate the kind of personal attack I had to sit here and listen to this afternoon.

I ask the minister to make a little better explanation of the regulations with regard to travel. The minister must admit that the city of Toronto, through its transportation commission and otherwise, has given his department a great deal of support, or he would not have been able to locate his plants where he did. Yet we in Toronto are getting little or nothing by way of concession. I have been asked to inquire whether the minister is not now able ta make some decision with regard to the fifty mile rule; and if not, can he not make some arrangement with the national railways about transportation, instead of continuing to rely on the old Noah's Ark cars which are utilized to and from Camp Borden on the national railways, while women are charged $2 and $2.40 and children $1.15 or thereabouts to visit the camps. Something should be done to relieve this situation.
The official oposition has given the government pretty good support, much better support than it deserved in the light of some of the answers which have been returned by one minister to questions asked by us on matters of public importance, questions designed to strengthen and support the government in a constructive way.
I ask the minister if he cannot give us some reply with regard to the provision of gasoline and rubber. An appeal was made last Easter and is repeated on every public holiday to the public to refrain from travelling, and soldiers and their families are not allowed transportation facilities, yet when I look around the Toronto district I see large numbers of government officials, not members of the cabinet or of their own civil departments, but connected with controls and subcontrols, making free use of facilities denied to others. It is high time that we paid some attention to the men who are fighting overseas. All our home defence and defence at home organization will not amount to a snap of the finger in the winning of this war, in spite of the great expenditure it entails in gasoline and rubber and other necessary supplies. I ask the minister to confer with his colleagues and see whether something cannot be done to give the troops who are in the camps the proper means of getting home, instead of compelling them to walk along the highway thumbing rides while carry-

ing grips and perhaps a hundred pounds of equipment. The army is the forgotten agency.
I have been in some of the camps, and it is clear to me that this is so when one sees the large number of these men still walking around in winter clothing, with no facilities for getting to their homes either by the highways or on the trains. It is a strange state of affairs that we should allow these estimates to go through without a protest, and I protest now. Wars are won by soldiers and sailors and airmen fighting at the front, and when I see some of our army in their Little Lord Fauntleroy costumes on the street cars, it seems to me a reflection on the House of Commons that we allow such a state of affairs to exist, while private transport or the buses and trains are available for civilians and booked by controls weeks ahead, and the railways are making fabulous sums. See what happened when the delegates of the empire parliamentary union arrived last evening at the depot. Between two trains, one coming in and one going out, without any guidance for passengers, hundreds of people might have been killed between the two tracks so close to both trains. When you make a complaint you cannot get results but you are told that you are making a personal attack.
I refer to this because I have seen something of the sufferings of the men in the army during the present war. I wish others could see what I have seen-women and children walking several miles to get on the trains. I do not wish to hold up the estimates, but I hope the three defence ministers and the Minister of Transport will take up this matter and see if something cannot be done, in dog days like these, to help the forces.

Would the minister tell us what is the average cost to the Canadian government of each of the several types of planes that are being manufactured in Canada? The ones I have in mind particularly are the Lysanders, the Harvards, the Ansons, the Mosquitos, the Hurricanes, the Tiger Moths and the Bolingbrokes.

I have not the costs here. Possibly I could get some of them. I have not the figures for the Mosquito or the Lancaster, as the costs of these planes have not yet been established. My hon. friend will understand that the production of at least 100 planes is necessary before production gets stabilized to the point where costs can be determined. Perhaps I can give him information on some of the other types of planes, but I do not happen to have that information here.
Could the minister give that to us to-morrow?
I will try.

I do not quite understand the attitude of some members on the government side in condemning the opposition for endeavouring to secure information regarding one of the largest items of expenditures parliament has to deal with, a matter of approximately $700 millions last year and an anticipated expenditure this year of $316 millions less reduction in revolving funds, together with hundreds of millions of dollars of expenditures for and on behalf of the British government. As a matter of fact, we do not properly examine the expenditures which are being made. We cannot do so, for we are invariably met with the type of answer given by the minister a few moments ago to the hon. member for Lethbridge, that the information in regard to costs is not available in certain particulars and regarding certain planes. Yet the minister, in answer to a question from myself, made the statement in the house the other day that we are producing planes in Canada at a price which would permit us to compete with the United States of America.
"Does" permit us.

That being so, there is only one way in which the minister is able to make such an optimistic statement, and that is on the basis of information which he has. As a matter of fact there is no organization in connection with the Department of Munitions and Supply which can so properly be called the department of mysteries and surprises as can this particular part of the department. I ask the government to visit the aeroplane plants in Canada, send investigators into those plants, talk to the employees free from any surveillance on the part of officials of the department or revelation to them of the information that they give, and, Mr. Chairman, they will tell a story of indifference, of laxity, and of inefficiency-

-in the production of aircraft in Canada.

We asked that there be conformity with experience and conformity with practical considerations in order to assure a large production of Anson planes. As a matter of fact, the minister in June, 1940, made certain predictions in regard to the production of Ansons. He did the same in November, 1940, and in February, 1941, he found that his predictions were not being fulfilled. No one has any argument to raise because of delays then. We realized the difficulties then. Today, with the expenditure that has been made in this connection, we feel that we have a right to demand that the maximum contribution which this country can make in the matter of fighting aircraft shall be made now, and that the excuses given in the past shall no longer be accepted. To-day we are asking not promises of production in the future but performance now in the fourth year of the war.
The minister said the other day that Canada was expending upon aircraft and the production of aircraft, 25 per cent of the total amount expended for war supplies, munitions and the like. I am going to ask him to place on the record the amount expended for aircraft in each of the years 1940, 1941, 1942 and
1943 to date for aircraft. In particular I should like to know how much money the government has invested in aircraft plants belonging to the government, first, for the production of aircraft, and second, for the production of parts. Finally, I would ask the minister for a statement showing month by month the expenditures made during the past year in the de Havilland plant and in the Malton plant for wages and general expenses. This information would be of much assistance.
I ask the minister in all seriousness this question. We have produced twenty-one fighting planes of the Mosquito type. Having regard to the fact that we have reduced to seven the number of types of planes we are producing, and regard being had to the months that have elapsed since production was first mooted, does not that record of twenty-one fighting planes produced indicate a lack of drive, a lack of appreciation of the necessity of fighting aircraft being produced now? Does it not indicate that a careful investigation should be made by the minister to the end that aircraft production should be encouraged and increased?
I realize that almost a year ago-on May 14, 1942, to be exact-the minister stated what the aircraft production of Canada had been up to that time-3,749 planes, as I remember. To-day our production is slightly over 8,000. At that time the minister said that production has now been stepped up to 400 planes a month, but that there were some plants not in production. So far as actual production is concerned the promise which the minister made last year has not been failed in. The position, however, in fighting aircraft is such that I feel something should be done to re-form the production of planes, to build up an attitude that does not exist to-day in the aircraft factories in this country, namely, a determination on the part of the men working there to produce at whatever the cost in hours and in effort. The lack is not in the men. The men working in the factories say that they have lost faith-not in the minister, but in those charged with this aircraft production programme. There must be some reason for this; otherwise it would not have become necessary last year to start- a morale building campaign in the aircraft plants of this country. Absenteeism in these plants is low and I submit that one way to build morale is to make it possible for the men who work in these factories to know what the issue is. All they require is direction and a goal, and they will endeavor to secure the greatest possible production of aircraft for combat purposes.
It is often said, Mr. Chairman that it is easy to criticize. It is not easy to criticize.

I should like to take just a few moments to discuss with the minister a question 1 raised in the house on a previous occasion. I think it is in order under item No. 5; it has to do with the development, the mining and the milling of the cobalt ores produced in Canada. On that occasion I called attention to the fact that at the present time we are importing cobalt ore from Africa, refining it and shipping the finished product to Britain as well as using it in essential war fields. In the meantime the ore that is being mined' in northern Ontario, particularly in the Cobalt camp, is being stock-piled at Deloro. I pointed) out previously that the company owning the refining plant at Deloro is, or was in the early years of the war, a member of an international cartel, of which the company now shipping its ore to Canada was also a member.
Cobalt is an essential mineral to-day, the civilian use of which has been forbidden, or at least restricted to the point where it is practically forbidden. In addition to the cobalt contained in these ores there is a considerable content of silver, nickel and arsenic, all of which are also essential minerals. These ores are being stock-piled; they are not being refined at the present time, because the only plant capable of refining these ores is engaged in refining the African cobalt ores. I understand that during the construction and equipment of the Shipshaw plant it was necessary for the United States government to provide approximately 26,000,000 ounces of silver to be used in place of copper, which would indicate that at the present time there is a demand for all the silver we can produce. Yet considerable quantities of this mineral are being stockpiled without being refined at all. I note also from the reports of two mining companies that they were instructed by the dominion government to institute a search for arsenic.

I would call the minister's attention to the arrangement under which the producers of this mineral sell their products to the Deloro company. To begin with, they receive no credit for any cobalt under eight per cent. Anything less than that goes for nothing. They receive no credit for silver content less than fifty ounces per ton.
