They receive no credit whatsoever for the arsenic content in the minerals.
I have here a list showing a shipment of six carloads of this ore sent by one company to the. refinery. All of this is stock-piled at the refinery^. In the six carloads the unpaid nickel, silver and arsenic content amounted to $4,168, an average of S65.50 per ton, for which the primary producer received no credit whatever. The six carloads amounted to sixty-five tons. The producers of the metal point out to me that on the basis of the 1940 production that camp to-day' is capable of producing or would on, the basis of the 1940 production produce, cobalt, silver, nickel and arsenic to the value of over one and a quarter millions of dollars a year, and that there is a ready market for every ounce of those materials. That revenue could be available to the camp, and the mineral could be available to our war effort, if some means
War Appropriation-Supplies

could be found of providing the camp with a small hundred-ton mill and a small twenty-five ton refinery. The only mill available to the producers operates only part of the year, and it is costly. I am told that because of the inefficiency of the mill, arising from the fact that it was built many years ago the producers pay an average of $2 per ton more than wmuld be necessary if an efficient mill were provided.
I am told, further, that there is a loss which makes it almost impossible for many producers in that camp to ship their products to the mill. Incidentally, the mill now in operation was formerly the property of the company which now owns the Deloro plant, namely, the O'Brien interests. I realize that restrictions must necessarily be imposed on the release of building materials. I do not submit this by way of criticism of the minister's department, or of his policy, but I would ask the minister to examine the situation, if he can find time. I believe he would realize more fully than I do the need of getting all essential Canadian .minerals into our war effort if it can possibly '.be done. It is unfortunate that during these war years none of these minerals is going into our war effort. I do not know what the solution would be, but I am asking the minister to survey the situation. I am told that if the minister's department were satisfied, after examining the situation, that such a mill will make a valuable contribution to our war effort, funds are available from the metal reserve control of the United States for just such purposes.
There is a feeling abroad that members of the cobalt cartel are using their influence to restrict the refining of this metal. It is well known that they used their cartel to restrict production and to set prices in pre-war years. I pass this information on to the minister- and may I repeat that it is without criticism, but only as a suggestion that he have the matter looked into, for what it is worth.

I have no biief for the plant at Deloro, but I know that that plant is the only one in the British empire which at the present time is producing steelite, and other materials which are essential to the war effort. Without the plant the war effort could not go on, and I know the minister will bear me out in that statement. Cobalt is what they have to have; the other materials are not so essential. Since the beginning of the war that plant has expanded greatly.
They are not using Canadian ores.
They are doing the work; it does not matter what kind of ore they are using. They are using ore, and they are producing what is needed for the war effort.
I am not criticizing that.

The hon. member acted as if he had stock in the mining company which produced the cobalt. I have no brief for the Deloro company, but I think these facts should be placed on record. Nickel, silver and arsenic are produced in many other mines, and I know from what I have been told by the manager of the Deloro plant [DOT]-a man who works twenty-four hours out of the twenty-four, who is never idle, and who is at his job morning, afternoon and night-that they are producing to the limit, and that they have to keep a stock of cobalt on hand at all times.
Before I sit down I should like to ask if it is not possible for the minister's priorities branch to release ball-bearings, pedals and other items necessary for the production of bicycles? The workers have to have them to go to work.

My department will release
anything they can get their hands on, but the components for bicycles are under quota which is fixed in the United States. AH we can release is the quota assigned to Canada.

Just to keep the
record straight I want to say to the hon. member for Peterborough West (Mr. Fraser) that I do not own one dollar's wrorth of stock in any mining company, nor am I interested in mining stocks. I do know a number of people who are interested in these properties at Cobalt and who are anxious to see them developed. I made no attempt to deprecate the work being done by the Deloro company; I take it they are doing a good job, but the ores they are refining are brought into the country. This plant is being used to capacity to refine imported ores, and I cannot see why there should not be an opportunity to refine Canadian ores. That is my point.

I am familiar with the
situation in relation to cobalt. I may say that it took an extreme effort on my part to provide the stock pile which is the only market for our cobalt ore. Cobalt is a world metal and the Deloro smelter is a customs refinery, the only one in the British empire for this particular ore, as has been stated to-day. The cheapest source of ore happens to be South

War Appropriation-Supplies
Africa, where it is a by-product of another operation. Great Britain requires supplies of cobalt, and she chooses to buy the ore in South Africa, ship it to Canada for smelting and take the product. The only manner in which Canada touches the ore is to transport it across the country to smelt the ore. Cobalt is not a scarce article at the moment; there is plenty of it. My hon. friend is quite, wrong when he says that someone here is stopping the metal reserve from financing a mill. As a matter of fact we explored this with the metal reserve, at a time when we were under the impression that the supplies of cobalt were not adequate, but we were told that supplies were adequate. As a matter of fact the metal reserve is not interested in obtaining cobalt in Canada, since they have their own supply.
The camp which produces this is the old silver camp near the town of Cobalt. The price of silver dropped, the mines were old, the cost of producing the metal is up, and this camp is now in a bad situation. I wish the men who are mining cobalt ore would go over to Sudbury and help us mine nickel; that would be a much more useful war effort. However, as long as they insist upon mining cobalt ore we provide a market for it by way of a stock pile against some future need.

There is no break-down of this particular item, and it is rather difficult for one to know whether he is in order in discussing a certain matter. This item covers munitions production, aircraft production, ship production and miscellaneous stores. In my opinion too many of the answers given to the questions asked concerning the Department of Munitions and Supply have been given by the minister when relying upon his memory alone. It would have been much better if we had had accurate figures. I am thinking particularly of the figures we were given from time to time on aluminum. I know the minister has a good memory and I sometimes fall into the same trap myself and rely upon my memory rather than having the figures to back it up.
From time to time the first intimation we have of what is going on in Canada or in the minister's department comes from United States sources. As I have said before, there seems to be a policy of almost concealing what this country is doing in regard to certain matters.
We cannot afford press agents.

I have the Edmonton Bulletin of Saturday, June 19, which was sent to me by air mail yesterday. An article in this
issue is dated Washington and refers to statements given at a press conference by Robert Patterson, United States undersecretary of war, in connection with oil reserves on the Mackenzie river to supply fuel for the army and navy. He stated:
"It has been very successful," he said in reply to questions at a press conference about the oil development which has been a closely guarded military secret.
Then a large part of the story of the development in the Mackenzie area is told in the article. Reference is made to the construction of a pipeline, and to the fact that -numerous wells have been put down, almost all of which have been producers. A very fine oil field has been discovered. It seems to me that the minister and the government would be wise to take this house into their confidence from time to time with regard to such matters rather than to have the information seep through from our neighbours to the south. I know the first intimation I got of the aluminum contract was through an article which appeared in the New York Times last January.
I should like the minister to tell us something about this great development in the north country, a development in which some of us have been much interested. I have referred to it several times, and we have had long discussions about the matter. As I say, I am not sure whether a discussion of this matter would be in onler under this item, but I think we should be told what methods have been adopted to develop this great oil field. As I stated before, the vicepresident of Standard Oil has said that this is the largest reserve supply of oil anywhere on earth. We are very anxious that it shall not be alienated from the people of Canada to corporations either in the United States or in our own country. We must insist that this great reserve of oil shall be developed in the interests of the public of Canada. At the opportune time I should like the minister to give us a statement elucidating what Mr. Patterson has said, either confirming or refuting the statement which appears in the Edmonton Bulletin and which has every appearance of being authentic.

As my hon. friend has said, this was a military secret. The head of a military department can talk about a military secret, but a mere Minister of Munitions and Supply has to keep a military secret if he is told it is a military secret. There is nothing new about oil at Fort Norman. There have been wells there for many years, but the difficulty has been that Fort Norman is an inaccessible point as far as Canada is
War Appropriation-Supplies

concerned. The production has been confined to what could be used in the immediate area. The boats plying the Mackenzie river have been using this oil for many years. The activities in Alaska, on the Alaska highway, and the requirements of northern aviation, have made production from this area interesting.
The field has been developed by an arrangement between Canada and the United States. Additional wells have been drilled and, as the article states, a pipe-line is to be constructed to carry the oil from Fort Norman to White Horse. A refinery is being built at White Horse.
Is this being undertaken purely by the government of the United States?

It has been carried out by arrangement between the government of the United States and the government of Canada, but the actual financing of the neyr development has been by the government of the United States.
And is the work being carried on by a Canadian oil company or by the Standard Oil Company or the Shell?

Chiefly, I believe, by the Imperial Oil company, by arrangement with the government of the United States. I may say the arrangement provides that after the war, I will not say all, but a considerable portion of the wells-at least half-become the property of the Canadian government, as they stand. If my hon. friend asks for a return, perhaps at this time the Department of Mines and Resources will give him the details of the arrangement.
As a matter of fact we withdrew it at the request of the Minister of Mines and Resources, who did not wish it divulged.
I know he could not do so before, but I think it may now be possible to give the information. I suggest it may be worth trying.
Thanks for the tip.

There is a fine oil field in the vicinity of Norman. I question very much whether it is one of the great oil fields of the world. I do not think there is anything to demonstrate that. It is a shallow field, and I doubt whether it will compare with the Turner valley as a source of oil. That is just a layman's view, from what I have been able to discover about it. Nevertheless it is a useful field. Whereas earlier it was inacces-

sible it is inaccessible no longer. There is a market for the product and the field is being developed accordingly.
It has been known for twenty or thirty years.
Yes, at least that.

Before the item carries, and subsequent to the discussion which has already taken place, I have a series of questions which will appear on the order paper, the basis of which is found in the Ottawa Citizen of yesterday. I appreciate the point which has been raised by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). The question gives me, and1 should give every Canadian, a good deal of concern, from the point of view that here is a huge development about to take place-
It is taking place.

-is taking place, yes, and we did not know a great deal about it until the United States authorities began to make an announcement regarding it. The article to which I have reference in yesterday morning's Citizen is dated from Edmonton, June 20, and reads as follows:
A huge war-time oil development in the Fort Norman area of the Northwest Territories, 400 miles northeast of Whitehorse, Y.T., is under way.
Captain Freeman C. Bishop, public relations officer for the northwest service command of the United States army, said the project probably will be completed this year.
The programme, rivalling the Alaska highway in scope, was started many months ago, but previously the development was hidden under a shroud of military secrecy.
In addition to scores of oil wells, a pipeline extending more than 1,000 miles from Whitehorse, Y.T., to the area will be completed.
Brig.-Gen. James A. O'Connor, commanding general in charge of the Alaska highway, is in charge of operations. He said the project had been made possible only through the unflagging determination of the troops and civilians employed.
Hoping to tap vast oil resources in Canada's northwest, now a military area under the control of the U.S. army, officials have sent huge amounts of equipment and aeroplane loads of workmen into the many oil bearing sections.
It does not tell us whether a Canadian company is developing it, whether the capital is Canadian or American, whether the United States government or the Canadian government is doing the work. The whole thing seems to be shrouded in mystery. We heard something about an aluminum cartel; here is what might appear to be an oil cartel.
The reason why I am a little exercised about this is that I go to Edmonton occasionally; all over this country Edmonton is talked' about as being the coming city of

War Appropriation-Supplies
Canada, and I believe it is. I was in a hotel lobby on one occasion and1 sat on the lounge beside a United States army officer, whose name I do not know. We got into conversation. He had been into the far north. He said, "You folks here have been asleep over the years." I talked to him about returning to the United States, and he said, "You don't think we are going back, do you? Why," he said, "we are going to stay right here; we are going to take over for you people." That is the remark he made to me.
The Minister of Munitions and Supply may say that certain things are guarded for reasons of military secrecy, but he has a tremendous responsibility in producing munitions of war, and yet we are so slow that military officials of the United States have to come over here to develop our resources. That is a condition which bothers a good many of us, and I believe there should be some explanation of it. I get sick and tired of being in a Canada which is always at the tail end of everything. It is about time this country took the initiative in some directions. Surely, with a land of abounding wealth, some initiative should be shown in developing these resources for the good of the Canadian people. Let us not remain behind any longer in regard to natural resources or any other matter. When conferences are held, ours is the weak voice crying in the wilderness after everybody else has spoken. It is about time Canada showed more assertion in some of these things. I suppose the minister's answer must be accepted as sufficient for the moment, but I urge the government to take. the initiative and be strong in connection with these issues; it would give Canadians a feeling that we are really getting somewhere. I protest against information on great national developments coming from other than Canadian sources when our own government has known right along that these things are happening, and yet we have not been informed about them.
There is, of course, also the question of to whom these developments will belong after the war is over, whether the people will have a share in their own natural resources, or whether private or alien controls will be so complete that little or no benefit will accrue to the Canadian people.

I
asked the minister before about tropical serge. The item comes under his department. The note I have before me is that the government is supplying the cloth and reserving it for the air force only. Why is that so? Is there a shortage of that material?

I am not aware of it. I think
I would be aware if the army, navy or air force had ordered anything from the Department of Munitions and Supply which the department had not furnished. If the army have ordered tropical suits they have been getting tropical suits, and likewise the navyv There is no shortage of that material. The hon. member spoke about the wartime prices and trade board. I have no knowledge of the activities of the board, which reports to the Minister of Finance, but I can assure my hon. friend that we are still able to give the navy, the army and the air force whatever they require in the way of clothing.

I wish to ask the minister a question with reference to a press dispatch that appears in the New Glasgow Evening News of the 18th instant. I am not going to read it, but it refers to a small yard that was operating at Pictou, where the keels for two tugs were being built for the Royal Navy. According to this dispatch, about thirty per cent of the work was finished; they had on hand ninety-seven per cent of the materials necessary to complete the job, and under orders of the deputy minister of munitions last Saturday the work at that yard was discontinued. There are eighty men affected. The reason given for discontinuing the job was that it would interfere with production at the main yard. I understand that this small plant was constructed at quite an expenditure by the Ferguson Brothers; these two nearly completed tugs are on their hands, and apparently there is no understanding as to whether they will be completed. It is said that they cannot be completed anywhere else. Has the minister any comments to make on the situation?

I am familiar with that situation. The contract for the two tugs was placed with the understanding that they would be built at Trenton, and it was not noticed immediately that there would be any difficulty at Trenton as far as labour was concerned. Some weeks later it turned out that the tugs were to be built by Ferguson Brothers at Pictou, which is a different situation. Pictou was a small village-I should not say village, but a small town-when the war broke out, and the government has built that town up into a fair-sized city to-day, having provided houses for two or three thousand workers and their families. All this was for the building of merchant ships. The Ferguson yard was formerly the only large industry at Pictou. A separation was made between the shipbuilding activity and the Ferguson yard, and the Ferguson yard was improved for the purpose of taking care of the repair of naval and mer-
War Appropriation-Supplies

chant ships. The yard is needed for that purpose. In assessing the repair capacity of Canada the Ferguson yard is counted as available. The Department of Munitions and Supply cannot agree that the Ferguson yard should be converted to the building of steel tugs. Steel tugs can be built in many yards m Canada which are not busy at the moment. The Ferguson Brothers were called to Ottawa, and we discussed the situation. It was explained to them that the capacity of their yard was required for other purposes and a mutually satisfactory arrangement was made for moving the material to other yards. The contract with Ferguson Brothers for building these steel tugs has been cancelled. It was an unfortunate mistake that the contract issued by the department should have been diverted in that way, but as soon as the mistake was discovered it was rectified. I assure my hon. friend that there is more work in Pictou to-day than there are men and women to do it. We have no facilities in Pictou which are not fully booked for the rest of the season.
I appreciate that, but what I cannot understand is that these tugs are thirty per cent completed and ninety-seven per cent of the materials necessary to complete them is on hand- v
They were not thirty per cent completed. They are more nearly ten per cent completed by actual cost.	.
Is that material to be left there?
No. It will be shipped to Montreal and the contract will be completed. I believe it is the Montreal drydock company who have the bulk of the contract.
The Ferguson yard is being utilized for other purposes?
For the repair of ships, yes.

The minister said
to-day that 1,850 Anson planes have been produced. What is the present cost of producing them compared with the cost in* 1941 or 1942?
The cost of producing Anson aircraft to-day is approximately $45,000. I do not know what it was in 1941.
Does the break-down given here include overhauling and repairing of engines used in the British empire training scheme operating in Canada?
To what figures is my hon. friend referring?
I am referring to the estimates we are now discussing.
Item 5?
Yes.

These are revolving funds. The costs of overhauling planes are not voted in the estimates of the department of munitions. They are voted in the estimates of the Department of National Defence for Air. These are simply revolving funds that finance the work from the time the plane is delivered to us for repair to the time it is paid for by the Department of National Defence for Air.

When the estimates
were before the Minister of National Defence for Air I asked about that, and that minister said it was under the department of munitions. That is why I asked.
That is correct.

There has been some discussion concerning the pipeline from Mackenzie river to White Horse and concerning the wells at Fort Norman. Is there any agreement between the dominion and the United States or any board under the United States government with regard to this pipeline? As the minister knows, there is either an agreement or an exchange of notes between the two governments in connection with the Alaska highway. Is there anything of that type in connection with this pipeline?

The proper place for my hon. friend to obtain that information is either the Department of External Affairs, .properly that department, or the Department of Mines and Resources. The Department of Munitions and Supply has had no hand in the negotiations, and it would be unwise and improper for me to make a statement about the transaction.
With regard to drilling for oil in northern British Columbia, what is the present situation?

The only drilling for oil in northern British Columbia that I know of is a well drilled by the provincial government, which I understand is not productive. So far as I know there is no other drilling.

There were negotiations
between the provincial government and the dominion government concerning the development of that field. Can the minister make a statement in regard to those negotiations?
No definite project has been brought to finality.

Under the estimates of the Minister of National Defence for Air I

TFar Appropriation-Supplies
asked a question about small boats to be built in Toronto in a plant now being built south of the Canadian Pacific railway tracks near Leaside. I understand the boat is made of some kind of plywood and is used as a crash boat in connection with aeroplanes.
I think they were light invasion barges. I understand it is the Howard Furnace company.
Yes.

We called for tenders on that boat and this company was low tenderer. The business was split between three companies.
I am not defending the wisdom of putting the Howard Furnace company into that business. It is one of those things that happen. The production committee approved the transaction. I must say that it was not drawn to my attention. However, as I say, the Howard Furnace company were low tenderer, and they are now on their way and, I believe, are doing good work. It is a lump sum contract.

I am glad to hear they are doing good work. I have known these people for quite a number of years and they are good furnace manufacturers. They know how to make and install hot air furnaces, and their furnaces have given good results. But when I saw that they had a contract for making boats of any kind, I just wondered how that came about. As the minister says, the matter did not come before him. I doubt whether a man of the minister's business experience would have given a contract for making boats to any hot air furnace manufacturer. It might just as well have been given to some farmer or egg producer. I hope the company makes a success of building these boats and makes some money out of it. But it is the sort of contract which makes the public wonder how the thing came about, especially when boat builders in Ontario are not running their plants at full capacity. I believe they are running at only 60 to 65 per cent of their capacity. Any one of the prominent boat-building companies on the Muskoka lakes or Georgian bay would have been glad to make these boats for the government. I think the minister ought to tell us why the men who let the contracts-[DOT] not the minister himself-let this contract for making boats to a hot air furnace company, when from 25 to 30 per cent of our present boat-building capacity is not being used.

All I can say is that every small boat builder in Ontario had a chance to tender on these invasion barges. The Howard Furnace company were willing to
quote a lower price than any other company.
I am not suggesting that all good judgment
was used in the transaction.

I am not quarrelling
with giving the contract to the lowest tenderer.
Mr. DIEFENBAIvER: There is one other matter I wish to bring to the attention of the minister. It has to do with a problem which has been discussed in the house on more than one occasion, namely, the production of alcohol from wheat. The minister dealt with this problem the other day at some length, and if I understood him aright the argument which he advanced against the use of wheat was that it would mean that the farmer would receive only 25 to 30 cents a bushel for the wheat so used. That argument has been used before. I know it was advanced in all seriousness by the minister, but I want to bring to his attention something which I think is worthy of his consideration.
I realize that for the time being a decision has been made on this question, and that the plant at Sarnia has been or is being established. But within the last few weeks a new process has been discovered in the United States which it is claimed will revolutionize the production of alcohol from wheat. I refer the minister to an article in Business Week of June 12, 1943. This is an authentic magazine, and the article says:
The chemnrgist's dream of grain alcohol as the answer to farm surpluses may yet come true- and -with it a lengthening horizon of post-war possibilities for the rubber, oil and chemical industries.
It goes on to point out:
Park and Tilford distillery company demonstrated the new process last week at a distillery in Brownsville, Pa.
This was a process which was discovered less than four months ago by Irvin W. Tucker, a young chemist in the department of agriculture of the United States working under the direction of Doctor A. K. Ball, chief of the department's enzyme research laboratory. They have been working on this process for a considerable period of time, and the difficulty of the price to the farmer for his wheat was apparent, as well as the problem of the utilization of the by-products. Yet within the past few weeks, according to this article-I am going to quote only a portion of it-a new era has come in prospect for the wheat producers. The article states:
With full development of the possibilities, grain alcohol can be reduced to the cost levels of molasses and synthetic alcohol, which are ordinarily about 50 per cent cheaper than grain alcohol. This would make large-scale production of grain alcohol for synthetic rubber and other

War Appropriation-Supplies

industrial purposes a practical post-war possibility, with tremendous implications for industry as well as for the farmer.
Heretofore, ehemurgists who grappled with the question of farm surpluses habitually stubbed their toes on two hard problems: There was no market for the tremendous volume of alcohol that could be produced from farm products, and the cost of farm alcohol was prohibitively high.
That was the point made the other day by the minister. The article goes on:
The war has solved the first problem-the synthetic rubber industry can use 250,000,000 gallons of alcohol annually, and there is more possibility that farm alcohol may be needed for motor fuel with petroleum reserves being depleted at global war rates. Ball and Tucker appear to have solved the second.
There is no more important problem than this. I think it is only fair to say that the members generally have not a knowledge of chemistry and of the possibilities of development in this industry to speak authoritatively upon it. The minister stated last night that the war was not being fought by Canada on the basis of provinces or provincial considerations, and with that, at the moment, I am not going to argue, but I feel that we in the western provinces have received too few war industries or industries established or bonused by the government through capital assistance. Our western provinces, and in particular Saskatchewan, have been depleted of a large percentage of their population because war industry has taken them out of those provinces, though not in the same large measure as enlistments for service in the armed forces. This problem of the production of alcohol will become intensified as time goes on and oil reserves are depleted. The minister has unreservedly given the government's approval to the production of rubber from petroleum, but his decision and his statement will not down the cry from all over western Canada for the solution of this problem by utilizing the wheat reserves.
I wish to offer to the minister a suggestion which I think is worthy of serious consideration. We in this house can never arrive at any definite conclusion in regard to this problem, not being possessed of the necessary knowledge of chemistry or the processes involved. In view of the fact that hundreds of millions of dollars have been advanced to industry in eastern Canada, with practically no such advances being made in western Canada, at least as far as Saskatchewan is concerned-as I have said on more than one occasion, the total of capital advances and assistance in that province does not exceed $1,000,000-in the interests of the farmer; in the interests of the liquidation of part of the large reserves of

wheat that we have on hand, would the minister give consideration to the appointment of a royal commission to investigate the whole problem? I do not suggest a commission composed of men unacquainted with the problem, but rather one composed of representative chemists, professors of chemistry and commercial chemists, who would look into the whole problem, and arrive at a scientific conclusion with respect thereto. When one reads an article such as that to which I have just referred, appearing in a most authoritative magazine, in which it is stated that this process can be and is being developed in the United States, and that it assures a fair and reasonable price for the farmers' wheat, it becomes a matter for serious consideration.
The setting up of such a royal commission would not be a costly process. Representatives of the chemistry departments of the different universities, industrial chemists and men of that kind could be convened, and during war time most if not all of them would give their services without cost to the state, with a view to contributing to the solution of a very important problem. I bespeak the minister's consideration for this suggestion. I think it would do much to clarify the atmosphere and the thinking of farmers all over Canada who believe that something should be done and that the reason why it is not being done is the attitude of the oil companies. I do not join in that view, though I mention it. By the setting up of a royal commission the whole problem could be considered; the various processes could be discussed and decided upon by men competent to deal with such matters and, if favourable findings were made by this commission and acted upon a very important contribution would be made to the welfare of the western provinces and to the dominion as a whole.

I would point out to my hon. friend that thorough study has been given to this matter already. He asks that a royal commission be appointed, but I would suggest that we have in Canada a permanent body, the national research council, which is set up exactly as my hon. friend suggests. It has scientists from industry and scientists from the teaching profession; it is the focal point for all the scientific knowledge in Canada, and in my opinion it is most ably administered. The president of the national research council was formerly dean of the university of Saskatchewan, which position he occupied for some twenty years or more. Therefore I suggest that he is not unfamiliar with the problems of the

War Appropriation-Supplies
west and not unsympathetic to those problems. The national research council studied this question thoroughly, but sooner or later a stage is reached when a decision must be made, and in this case the decision was made. Since that decision was made, the government has spent a good many million dollars in preparing to produce butadiene from petroleum. It is all very well to suggest that, having spent this money, we should set up a royal commission to say whether we should produce this commodity in some other way. We are building now, and we shall have enough capacity to meet our requirements. I cannot imagine that for a great many years we shall need butadiene in excess of the amount we are organizing to produce. Therefore what would be the purpose of a new study? Perhaps the decision was wrong; but the decision was made; action was taken, and it is very difficult to turn back the clock at this stage. I say the best scientists in Canada studied the question and arrived at the conclusion which the government is implementing. That decision having been taken rightly or wrongly, there is no purpose in reopening the subject at this time.

I find myself in considerable confusion following the remarks of the hon. member for Lake Centre. On the one hand we are told that every bushel of grain will be needed for food after the war, that millions of people in Europe are literally starving today. On the other hand we are told by some hon. members that the only way to dispose of our surplus grain is by spoiling it for human food. I speak as a farmer with forty years experience in western Canada, and I have a little knowledge of chemistry. I wish to say that this idea of turning prime human or animal food into inedible substances is simply the wrong economic solution. People are saying that the economic system under which we operate at the present time cannot provide a decent living for those who are producing the food of the world, and that therefore we have to take some of that food and turn it into chemical substances in order to create a shortage of food so that the price may be increased. It is the same old economy of scarcity. If this house and this country, or the world if you like, have not yet learned that it is possible adequately to reward people for performing the most fundamental of all services, then they have not learned anything, and the outlook for the world after the war is an extremely poor one. There is a proper way of doing this. It is not necessary to spoil food in order to make it scarce. Either there 72537-247*
are millions of people in Europe and elsewhere who are hungry, or all the propaganda we have been hearing is false. If that situation does exist, certainly we shall need all the food that can !be raised; and the price of that food or the reward to the growers of it is not a question of chemistry but a question of economics, and, I might say, of finance. Monetary reform; that is the solution, not chemurgy.

May I ask a question
respecting the processing of wheat into butadiene and alcohol. I understand there have been certain recent developments in that process which might change the picture from what it was at the time the government made its decision. Have there been such developments?

I know of no development
which would have changed the decision, had we been making it to-day. The government maintains an experienced chemist as liaison officer in Washington, who keeps in close touch with chemical developments in the United States. I receive his reports from time to time. Then, our own officers are studying the position intensively. I know of no recent scientific development which would have changed the decision, had we been making it to-day. I think the decision if made to-day would be the same one we made some twelvemonths ago.

Apparently employees on
the third shift, which is known as the graveyard shift, in shipyards on the Pacific coast are paid on the basis of nine hours' pay for seven hours' work, whereas those who are engaged in the Boeing plant, in connection with aircraft production, are paid on the basis of eight hours' pay for seven hours' work. Is it the policy of the government that there should be the same treatment in all war industries? Why should there be that difference?

The policy of the government is that labour courts have been established to decide wages in every industry. The courts have given their decision with respect to the shipbuilding industry, and the aircraft industry, for reasons which they no doubt found equitable. The government has nothing to do with wages. Wages are determined either by the national war labour board or by regional war labour boards, and the government, the manufacturers and labourers themselves are bound by those decisions.

Has that resulted in the
same difference between the practice in shipyards and aircraft plants right across Canada?

War Appropriation-Supplies
I cannot say as to that; but I think my hon. friend would do well if he would do what everyone else does, namely, let the courts decide.

I understood the minister to say an amicable settlement had been made or was to be made between the Pictou shipyards and the department with respect to the dispute in connection with tugs. Was the minister referring to Ferguson Brothers?
Yes.

I asked the minister if he would bring to the house to-morrow the prices the Canadian government is paying in Canada for various types of aircraft, and he intimated he would do so. Would he at the same time bring the prices the United States government is paying for the same kind of aircraft in the United States?

I cannot bring the latter information, I am sorry to say, because I do not have it. I can give the hon, member the prices we are able to determine at this time. As I said, the Mosquito and the Lancaster are just coming into production, and a sufficient quantity has not been made to determine prices. However, I can give some prices of other types of aircraft. As I said a while ago, the Anson costs $45,000; the Tiger Moth, $4,800; the Bolingbroke, $62,500; the Lysander, $28,600; the Harvard, $20,000, and the Hurricane, $33,750. These prices are plus sales tax.
And including engines?
Yes.

I asked several
questions this afternoon which I realized the minister would not be able to answer immediately. Would he answer them to-morrow?
I shall look through Hansard, and if I can furnish the information I shall be glad to table it.

I have not yet received a reply to my question respecting the poundage of plane production in each year. The minister indicated that there had been a considerable increase, and I should like to have the yearly record.
I shall furnish that,

There is a matter I should like to bring to the minister's attention, and *concerning which I would ask for some information. I refer to the manufacture of Bren guns. In his statement on June 11, as reported at page 3545 of Hansard, the minister

said that the maximum output of Bren guns would be 8,000 a month, which will be reached this month, and will be maintained at that rate until the end of 1944.
I do not think the full information respecting Bren guns has come out, and perhaps in answering my question the minister may be able to satisfy the committee. Has the Bren gun plant during the past year, or the past few months, spent a considerable amount of money to raise the production of that plant to 10,000 rather than 8,000 a month? The minister's statement would mean that instead of a maximum production of 10,000 a month, the reduced amount is now 8,000, and that that number will be maintained until the end of 1944.
I believe it is well known throughout the country that in respect of war contracts, and particularly those having to do with gun production, any reduction in contractual obligations has arisen from a readjustment of British contracts. While the reasons for those reductions need not be discussed here, the fact remains that such reductions would have entailed the transfer and change in employment of a good many men in the plants involved. The minister's statement that 8,000 would be produced until the end of 1944 indicates that at least to some extent the production of Bren guns is being turned from the British contract to a contract for some other country. That brings me to the point connected with the utilization of mutual aid funds. A billion dollars has been appropriated under the mutual aid bill for the purpose of providing war supplies for other countries. Having in mind the fact that there is a contraction in the obligation which this country must now fulfil to Great Britain, would the minister indicate whether there has been some recent arrangement under which the Bren gun plant, and other plants, have now been kept at their normal output by virtue of utilization of part of that billion dollar fund? That being the situation, I think the minister ought to give the committee information with respect to what part of the reduction in the British contract is being taken up by the utilization of the billion dollar fund. I think the minister and hon. members have read that part of the billion dollar fund is being used to take up the slack, if one may use the ordinary term, of these contracts with Britain which have been subsequently cancelled. At her press conference Madame Chiang Kai-shek referred to a matter, which was referred to subsequently in the debate by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), namely, the urgent need by China of aircraft. The minister has referred to the expansion which has taken

War Appropriation-Supplies
place in the production, of aircraft, and I should like to know if China or other countries have asked for this extra output which would seem to be available by reason of the restrictions in the British contract. Or are we utilizing part of the billion dollar fund for the purpose of keeping our men employed and our plants operating?

I can say at once that we are not carrying on any production for the sake of providing employment. I wish I could get
35.000	or 40,000 men to-day from plants where they are not needed. I would certainly close down any such plants immediately because I know exactly where I would put the men thus released. We do not keep plants going for the sake of employment. My hon. friend is quite mistaken about the contracts in the past for the production of Bren guns. The output of the Bren gun factory has not been going exclusively to England. A large part of it has gone to our own troops. Bren guns have been sent to China, the Philippines, to Australia, to New Zealand. Our production is governed by the combined production and planning board. This board assesses the need for products all over the world and decides how much will be made in Canada, in England and in the other producing countries, and the manufacture is arranged accordingly. Distribution is taken care of by the munitions assignment board; when the guns are made they are assigned to each government by that board. That is the ordinary procedure.
The production of Bren guns has been stepped up continually since the war began. I believe the original rate of production was
5.000	a year. We had an objective of 3,000 a month which we thought would meet the demand, but further pressure was exerted to increase the production, and it has been increasing each month. We have never reached a production of 8,000 a month, but w'e have passed the 7,000 a month mark. Two other types of automatics were made in the plant, the Colt-Browning and the Boys antitank rifle. We thought of stepping up the production of Bren guns to 10,000 a month by converting certain machinery w'hich had been used to manufacture these other types. However, a study of the situation indicated that this would be more than the allied needs, and we levelled our production at 8,000 a month. A production of 8,000 Bren guns a month would seem to meet the requirements of the war as they appear at the present time.
Have any men engaged in the production of Bren guns been laid off?

I cannot say what the men were working at, but the number of men and women engaged in the production of Bren
guns is greater to-day than it has ever been, A certain number of men who were producing Bren guns two or three months ago may have been laid off for the reason that they had low seniority. The lay-off took place on a plantwide seniority basis. While I am on my feet. I should like to correct a statement I made a few moments ago. I stated that the cost of the plane included the cost of the engine, but it does not. The costs I gave do not include the cost of the engine.
How many plants in Canada are devoted exclusively to the manufacture of machine tools?
There are a number.
Many dozens.
I think perhaps that is true.
Is Canada equipped to manufacture the machine tools which will enable her to change over from war production to peace production?
Yes.
The minister said that he could use 35,000 to 40,000 men. In what industries would he use them?

I would start with the highest priority industries and go down the line. I would start off with the aeroplane industry, and the naval shipbuilding industry; I would straighten out the flour-milling situation at Peterborough and give the General Electric the 600 men they need. I would go into the base metal mines and bring them up to the strength they should be, and I would give some help to coal mining and lumbering.
Is there a shortage of man-power in the aircraft industry?
Yes. It is still expanding and it needs more men.
When was Toronto Shipbuilding taken over as a government company, and what has been the production record of hulls and completed vessels?

This company has completed sixteen Bangor minesweepers.

This afternoon the minister gave us additional information in connection with housing, and he has accounted for $43,000, which reduces the cost of the unit of
War Appropriation-Supplies

fifty houses nearly $1,000 per unit, as he explained it, but I must say that the information he has given does not clear the situation. He mentioned last evening, as reported in Hansard, at page 3853:
The hon. member for Mackenzie has given rather an Alice in Wonderland picture of the costs of these developments. He seems to be wholly confused by the returns he obtained.
I must admit, Mr. Chairman, that I am even more confused since the minister gave his information to-day. He gave us a table for the 100 houses showing the average cost to be $2,939.87; that is the figure he gave last night; but the extras in connection with these houses, to provide sewers and streets and so forth, average $995.48 per unit, whereas last evening, in answer to a question, he stated the average in Hull was about $760 per house. Last night he gave the cost of the two-bedroom house as $1,889.13, and this afternoon he gave the cost as $1,980.78. There is a difference there of about $100 per house, and no explanation is given as to whether the figures reported last night were wrong or those read this afternoon were wrong. Then, extras in connection with these fifty houses average $828.68; and as I pointed out before, the minister gave $760 last night as the cost of the extra services. I submit that it is the minister who has given us an Alice in Wonderland picture, and I would appreciate it if he would have his officials make a further study and tell us whether the figures he gave this afternoon, or the ones he gave last night, or some others, are the ones we are to accept.

The department has made three returns on the subject. All three are correct with one exception: one return was not corrected for the money that was spent in Hull on the Ottawa project. If my hon. friend will make that correction he now has the final figures of the whole project, which are entirely consistent with the three returns which were handed down in this house. I do not know that I can do any more for him except give him the final figures as we have recorded them here.

Except that last night the minister stated, as reported in Hansard, at page 3853:
In connection with the Hull project . . . for the two-bedroom houses, it was $1,889.13.
This afternoon he brought down information that the costs of the fifty houses totalled $99,039.07, which gives an average for the fifty of $1,980.78. Either the minister was wrong last night, or he was wrong this afternoon. I hope that in due course he will tell me on which occasion he was wrong.

There were two types of house in the fifty-house project. I gave the cost of the small house. As the return shows which I put on Hansard this afternoon, it is called style No. 1, and the average cost was $1,897.78; as to style No. 21, of which twenty-five were built, the cost depends on the interior finish, but it varies between $2,065.56 and $2,073.76. The figure my hon. friend has taken is the average of the fifty houses, and he has an average house there which is neither type No. 1 nor type No. 21, but is a composite of the two. If he will take into account that in the fifty there are twenty-five of one type and twenty-five of another, he can reconcile the figures.
The figure of $1,889.13 which the minister gave last night was the average for the fifty.
No; I gave it as the cost of the small house.
I wish the minister had made that clear last night.
I make it clear now.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Carried.

I am prompted to rise at this moment if for no other reason than the anxiety of my hon. friend across the way. I wanted to ask the minister whether this item covers storage of materials which are -on this side of the water awaiting transfer overseas.
Yes. I can give my hon. friend the break-down if he would be interested.
I would.

It includes a number of items: First, subsidies to private contractors. I might say that certain coal industries and certain freight rates in the steel industry are subsidized by the department. That is one item. Then, payments to municipalities: that is for services to a municipality rendered in the event that the industry itself does not pay taxes.
Would the minister give the amount of each of these items?

Yes.
Subsidies to private contractors; estimated subsidies for 1942-43, $6,675,665.98, of which there was actually expended S4.294,793.80.

War Appropriation-Supplies
Payments to municipalities, estimate last year $561,965.65., actual expenditure $219,696.73.
Machinery transfers; that is transfers of machinery owned by the crown from one plant to another plant; the estimate of that Last year was $10,000, and the actual expenditure was $1,248.73.
Patent rights: the estimate for last year was $1,000,000; instead of an expenditure last year there was actually a revenue of $187,889.49.
Experimental and development costs: the item provided was $2,418,837.50, and the actual expenditure was $474,304.55.

Would experimental
costs have to do with the matters which the minister referred to this afternoon, namely the research council, or is that an additional amount?

It is in connection with army engineering design, which is carried out for the army by the Department of Munitions and Supply certain testing in the development of army vehicles, and some development work which is carried out for us by the research council, for which we pay; and expenditures of that sort.
Does that cover investigation into private inventors' plans and devices?

No. Private inventors' plans are examined by the inventions board, which is not in the Department of Munitions and Supply. I had better furnish the remainder of this break-down, since I am at it.
The next item is operation of storage warehouses: there was an item of $2,000,000,, and actually there was a revenue of $52,400.58, instead of an expenditure.
Other production expenses: estimate, $1,181.057.33 actual expenditure $927,275.80.
