In other words, if we buy components in the United States they enter Canada duty free for the United Kingdom, but the mechanics of the thing is that we actually pay the duties and then deduct them from the invoice price to England and charge them to this account. It represents Canadian duties paid on United States imports which later went to Britain.
Publicity campaigns in connection with rubber and fuel: estimate $675,750.43; expenditures, $322,182.51.
Has the minister an itemized account to show how that amount of $372,000 is made up?

I have the information, but perhaps I may be allowed to put these figures on Hansard first.
Operation of chartered vessels: appropriation $435,944.83; actual expenditure, $145,111.02.
Gasoline rationing plan:	appropriation,
$1,800,000; actual expenditure $938,601.95.
Administration of government-owned companies: $4,000,000 appropriation; actual expenditure, $1,496,740.84.
Loss through cancellation of contracts: appropriation, $10,000; actual expenditure, $3,746.30.
Protective measures; oil storage; appropriation, $85,000; actual expenditure $82,148.68.
Last year's appropriation was $35,854,221.72, of which we expended $14,300,408.74. The item this year is $15,000,000 odd of which $5,000,000 is a revote.

As regards subsidies to municipalities, has the department any general policy of compensating municipalities where a property has been expropriated-I have a particular instance in mind

where a crown company has been formed to take over the operation of the plant itself. In these cases, as the minister knows, some serious complications sometimes arise on the question of loss of revenue to the municipalities. What is the department's policy in general with regard to crown companies which are replacing those that have been tax-paying institutions previously?

If the ownership of the property passes to the crown, the property is of course tax-free under the British North America Act, and nothing can be done about that. But if services are rendered by the municipality to the plant itself, it is the custom to pay for them. The payment is payment for services, not payment in lieu of taxes. It is an equitable payment for services rendered.
What are the companies and private contractors to whom subsidies were paid in connection with the $4,000,000 odd? What are the quantities of coal moved, and where?

The largest item is in connection with the Dominion Steel company. Its ore is at Wabana, and the transportation costs have to be paid. It has also to move coal to its destination up the St. Lawrence. That movement has been seriously interrupted by the war. As hon. members know, a number of
War Appropriation-Supplies

boats owned by the Dominion Steel Company *-all the boats-have been sunk by enemy action. The boats now operating carry a very high war risk insurance rate, and in order to make operations of the plant possible, an agreement was entered into about eighteen months ago to the effect that the dominion government, as a subsidy, would compensate the company for increases in the cost of water movement of its raw materials and finished product. That payment last year amounted to, I believe, about $3,000,000.
That is the Dominion Steel and Coal?

Yes. In addition, certain coal mines in the west have been subsidized to some extent, for opening up new operations or for improving the output of their coal. I have not the break-down of these payments. The emergency coal production board hears the applications for subsidies and recommends the application, or otherwise, to the department. If a recommendation is made by the board and it receives the approval of the department, the subsidy is paid.
What was the value of the material moved by the Dominion Iron and Steel Company on which the subsidy was paid?

Iron ore and limestone from Newfoundland and Sydney, and coal moved up the St. Lawrence, would run into a very large figure. I cannot say what the amount would be, but it w'ould be in the order of fifteen or sixteen million dollars.

This item includes charges for warehousing. When, one sees these goods stored beside railway tracks in different parts of the country and in all sorts of weather, one wonders why that material is not put under cover. I suppose that question has been given thorough consideration by the minister, but could he tell us why it is not possible to protect these goods from the weather? Do they not depreciate greatly by being left out all winter?

No; the goods do not depreciate. The service vehicles will see much rougher usage after being uncrated than they do while they are in crates, and if there are a few spots on the enamel that is not a very serious matter for war vehicles. The vehicles are well and substantially packed, and I can assure my hon. friend that no damage results from storing them alongside the railway tracks. He realizes that the normal stock of vehicles is about 30,000. Our people advise
TMr. Howe.]
me that they cannot fill their shipping orders with stocks of much less than that, which represents a little less than two months' output. If stocks get over fifty thousand, as they did on one occasion, we get disturbed. But thirty thousand we consider normal.
I would point out to the minister that his general statement is probably quite all right. But as a matter of real fact many thousands and thousands of dollars worth of these goods-[DOT]
Millions.

My hon. friend
suggests millions. I am being conservative and saying that many thousands and thousands of dollars worth of these goods are stored alongside the railway tracks, exposed to the weather and with the packages broken. To my own knowledge, in the area fronting on the Don river, thousands and thousands of dollars worth of spare parts to replace the springs on vehicles 'which were recently used in the North African campaign are lying there exposed to the weather and have been for months. Even rubber tires are lying there exposed to the weather and have been for many months. No doubt they are destined to be replacement parts on vehicles at present in combat areas. But there is no doubt in my mind or in the mind of anyone with ordinary common sense that these goods are perishing.	,
I am rising on this occasion not so much to criticize the handling of these goods as to point out to the minister and to those charged with the responsibility for taking care of these thousands and thousands of dollars worth of goods that this exposure to all kinds of weather affects these spare parts considerably, and that consideration should be given by those responsible to the depreciation which is taking place in these goods. I can readily understand that there are difficulties in unloading and storing these goods, because it is a new venture for the carrier company and warehousing is not provided. These goods have accumulated as a war-time necessity. At the same time, however, I should like to put on record as a constructive criticism that something should be done to protect the many, many thousands of dollars worth of these goods from the damage which is now being done to them on account of the inadequate warehousing facilities, those facilities being on the ground by the side of the tracks.
I know it is impossible for the Department of Munitions and Supply to have spare parts

War Appropria lion-Supplies
for every type of equipment overseas always ready for shipment. I know the difficulty in getting bottoms to transport these goods across the ocean, but in the interests of economy a review should be made of the entire inventory of spare parts lying alongside the tracks all across Canada, because the goods are at present depreciating to an extent which those responsible are perhaps not cognizant of. I refer particularly to the area with which I am perhaps better acquainted, from Windsor through to Montreal, where there are thousands and thousands of dollars worth of goods stored alongside the tracks and perhaps without any destination. I saw the word "Egypt" on many, many hundreds of these packages, some of which were broken, some in a state of disrepair, some spoiling, some depreciating. Some of these goods have been stored alongside the tracks for a period of two years.
It must be remembered that the original destination of these goods may be changed. I realize the difficulties of the department in getting furtherance orders with regard to these goods, because there are no bottoms available in which to ship them. At the same time, however, as a matter of economy in taking care of this costly investment, someone within the minister's department should give consideration to whether these goods are not going to be destroyed through exposure to the weather and depreciation to an extent that they may not be serviceable if and when they eventually reach their destination.
I realize the other difficulty. While these spare parts stored in Canada in the wide, open spaces have depreciated, they may not find their destination in the areas where the original machines of destruction for which they were intended as spare parts were used. The department would be well advised to take an inventory of what is lying out in the open all across Canada to replace as spare parts equipment that has already been shipped by way of Egypt for the North African campaign. These goods may never be used now in North Africa. Their original destination may be changed. I am of opinion that perhaps many scores of thousands of dollars worth of goods lying out in the open in Canada without warehouse covering, but lying as warehouse goods under this particular vote, might be reclaimed for shipment to other theatres of war where they could be used. Perhaps many thousands of dollars worth of equipment has been shipped to the United Kingdom, and we may even find ourselves short of replacement parts for this equipment. We hope that the North African campaign is over, and these goods lying along the track branded "Egypt" may never have to go to Egypt. Could they
not as a matter of economy be brought back into supply for some other destination for which we are at present manufacturing supplies?
I am of opinion that this tremendous investment of Canada should be reviewed and an inventory taken, so that the department would know what they have available and what is not necessary for shipment to Egypt and the North African campaign.
Therefore the question I would direct to the minister is this: Has he recently had before him a review of this entire situation, representing a tremendous investment on the part of Canada, and has he any concrete plan for bringing into the asset side of our war effort this tremendous inventory of goods which are at present stored in Canada, some of which might be usable in a present theatre of war. and very much of which I am afraid is depreciating rapidly and should be brought back into supply to service equipment which has already been shipped overseas by the Department of Munitions and Supply?
I would be sorry, Mr. Chairman, if hon. members supposed that these goods were simply placed beside the track and forgotten.

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, I am not going to have the minister put in my mouth words which I did not say. I did not make the statement that the goods were put beside the track and forgotten. I was doing my best to offer a constructive criticism, and I rarely say anything unless I know what I am talking about. I did not suggest for a moment that they were put there and forgotten. I suggested that they were there now., and that since we had wTon the battle of North Africa there would be no necessity of sending more of these spare parts to that theatre of war. I was trying to make a constructive suggestion in that regard, and I ask the minister not to put in my mouth words that I did not utter.

My hon. friend is much too sensitive. Certainly I did not intend to put words in his mouth, and I did not think I was doing so. However, there seems to be an impression abroad that we do not have inventories of these goods, that we simply leave them there and let nature take its course. That is not true. We have an organization, headed by a man of great experience in charge of stored goods, not only automobiles but other goods that are stored, and periodic inspections are made.

Just stir up the head of that organization a bit, to see that he is on the job.
War Appropriation-Supplies

I can assure my hon. friend that every week I have an inventory of the goods in store in Canada. It is not an inventory that deals with small figures; it runs into very large figures. We do try to keep our inventories within reasonable proportions, and if we find too large an accumulation we apply for more shipping, which we usually get.
That organization was formed only this year, since January 1, was it not?
We had men doing the work before that, but we set up a more formal organization perhaps a year ago.

I
believe they have been checking all these deposit places only this year.

Nevertheless we maintained inventories before that. In the matter of spare parts, I may say there is no guesswork in that connection. No vehicle leaves this country without a standard list of spares. I do not think Canada needs to take off her hat to any other country making motor vehicles in the way we have kept up our spare lists. The manufacturers would much rather supply finished vehicles than parts, and it has taken a good deal of pressure to keep our spares up with our vehicles. When a vehicle is put on board ship a complete set of spares for the .required period, usually one year, is forwarded with the vehicle to the same destination and on the same boat. I can say also that no vehicle leaves these shores without a final inspection by the inspection board of the United Kingdom and Canada, and there is no danger whatever of a defective vehicle being put on board ship..
I think the damage suggested here has been greatly exaggerated. I know of very little damage and of very few claims for damage to goods. These goods are stored for the account of the owner. I may say that each vehicle as it comes out of the factory, is destined for a certain owner; it is built to fill a certain order. We have certain crates marked for Egypt that have not gone to Egypt; nevertheless the vehicle is what is called a desert-type vehicle in that it has sand tires, is fitted with sand-proof bearings and has certain other characteristics for desert work. It may be true that the fighting is over in North Africa, but perhaps it can be assumed that desert fighting in this war is not over. In any event the desert vehicle is a better made vehicle than the standard,

and if it is not required for desert fighting it will be accepted gladly for any other type of fighting.

There is one matter I should like to bring to the attention of the committee; it may not come strictly under the heading of general production and warehousing expenses; but since it has not been discussed already, I thought I might bring it up now.
Before doing so, however, since I have not previously taken part in the discussion of the munitions and supply items, I should like to take this opportunity of joining with other hon. members in congratulating the minister upon the great work he has accomplished. There has been some criticism of certain features of the work of his department, but I think members of this house and the great majority of the people of Canada realize that he has performed a magnificent task in bringing Canada's production to the high peak it has attained.
The matter to which I should like to refer is the giving of an award for great accomplishments in the manufacture of materials vitally needed for the winning of the war. There is no doubt that the manufacturing concerns of this dominion have performed a task which most of us thought impossible of achievement when the war started, and I think we should give credit to the executives of these manufacturing concerns as well as to the working men and women who have carried on in these plants. I know in the city of Brantford there are many elderly men who have spent long hours in the munition plants in order that our output might be the very greatest possible. These working people have not hesitated to labour very long hours, often at great sacrifice and to the detriment of their own health. The executives and workers of these companies take great pride in what they have accomplished; they rejoice in their achievements, and I believe some award might be given them. In our fighting forces awards are given for great achievements, for outstanding accomplishments and for heroic acts. This might be applied to the manufacturing concerns of our country. I believe in the United States there is an army and navy E award given to companies which achieve a certain high standard of production. My suggestion to the minister is that in Canada a high standard might be set and that those companies which attain such high standards should receive a reward. This reward might consist of a flag to be flown from their buildings, while each man in the plant might receive a pin bearing some symbol which

War Appropriation[DOT]-Supplies
would designate great accomplishment. I know the executives and working men would welcome such an award. It would be something toward which they could strive. I believe it would1 stimulate production, and would keep morale high in such companies. At the present time the company which is not doing a good job is not differentiated from the company which is doing an outstanding job. If some such award as I have suggested were given for great achievement, I am satisfied it would help much in our war effort.

I do not rise to speak critically of the government; far from it. But I must point out that the people of this country are aware of the vast expenditures made in peace time on our two great railway systems, as they serve on land, and through their steamship connections. The people in your constituency, Mr. Chairman, and in many other constituencies throughout the country, along the rights of way and branch lines of the two railway systems, are very much disappointed in these days with those systems. They see the line-up of package freight and munitions which has existed for a very long time, and into this fourth year of the war. When all these munitions are required to fight the enemy where the enemy is to be found, the people of Canada are wondering what they are getting for their money.
A return to the house has shown that down to the end of 1940, one year and three months after the outbreak of war, the Canadian National Railways had received two billion and a half dollars and the other system about twenty-five per cent more. That is more than they made in the whole four and a half years of the great war. I do not blame the minister for this condition. But I must say those who are overseas are wondering about the reason for this congestion. What is the object of it? Have matters which have come before the house, such as the plebiscite, and the difficulty of deciding the position of the theatre of war, held up these shipments? We may talk as much as we like about this matter, but the people back home in our constituencies see these goods along the rights of way of the two transportation systems. I am very much discouraged when I think of this. The soldiers overseas do not believe in it; and there should be an investigation into it. The two transportation systems are falling down all along the line.
For instance, let us consider the passenger service the two railway companies are giving us. Where is the railway commission, when all this is going on? Under the act they should operate in peace and war, but they have not done one thing to regulate this freight lying
along the rights of way of the railways. Home defence does not amount to anything, when it comes to beating Hitler. These munitions are required overseas, and if we hand these supplies to home defence, it will not amount to the snap of a finger in beating Hitler. Hitler will rejoice when he sees what is going on in this country.

I was told that the reason why these goods were lying along the railways was that there was a lack of ocean shipping facilities. On account of the length of time the goods have been there, are any of them now obsolete?

No, the goods are not obsolete. As I said some time ago, the practice is to use Canada as an area for accumulating necessary supplies for movement into a new area. As I stated earlier, prior to movement in North Africa we had very large stocks of goods in Canada, including motor cars. The boats which moved to Africa were loaded largely in Canada, and our stocks were sharply reduced at that time. I have no doubt that, if another invasion effort takes place, Canadian stocks will be heavily drawn on again.
In the early stages of the war the practice was to move goods from Canada to Great Britain, and to use Great Britain as storage ground. That is no longer being done. There are accumulations here which may be large or which may be small, depending on the state of the war. But they are part of the general strategy. They are by no means overlooked. I think there has been some exaggeration as to the length of time that any considerable number of items has been in storage in Canada. I am quite sure no article has been here as long as two years, standing alongside railway tracks.

I was interested to hear the Minister of Munitions and Supply state that Dominion Iron, Steel and Coal were subsidized for 1942 to the extent of $3,000,000. I am not objecting to the payment of these subsidies, provided they serve the purpose for which they are intended. I find an interesting statement in the Financial Post of June 12. I do not know whether the minister saw it or not, but it is captioned "Dominion Coal Seeks Subsidy", and it leaves one something to think about. The following appears at page 18:
Government auditors are now perusing the 1942 statement of Dominion Coal Company to check its claim for special subsidy treatment under the emergency coal production board.
Although it mined 67,000 fewer tons of coal in 1942 than in 1941, it improved its financial position in marked degree-presumably as a
War Appropriation-Supplies

result of the government having underwritten production to the extent of "standard profits" or 15 cents a ton-whichever was the smaller item.
I understand these subsidies are paid, and a new subsidy is being sought from the emergency war production board, with the end in view of increasing production. According to this statement, if these figures are correct, in 1942 while there was a substantial increase in the subsidy paid to that company it mined
67,000	fewer tons of coal than had been produced in the previous year. The statement goes on to say that after depreciation and depletion, from zero to $1,250,000, and after paying what must have been normal increased taxes-because in 1941 with a net loss there could have been no tax paid worth mentioning-the company showed a net profit of $469,618 as against a 1941 loss of $566,125. I am leaving out the tax question. The improvement in the company's position was $2,285,000.
I am now interested in finding out how much of that $3,000,000 was subvention, and how much of it was paid by way of subsidies. Second, I would ask the minister to comment on the observation that the government is underwriting standard profits for that company to the extent of fifteen cents a ton. If the purpose for which these subventions and subsidies are paid is to increase production, rather than to put figures on the right side of the balance sheet of the coal company to the extent shown in this article-an improvement in their own financial position, with a loss in production of 67,000 tons-it would be well for the government now, in the light of the application for new subsidies, to make an examination of the question of subventions with the end in view of guaranteeing that that money will be spent this time in a way which will increase production.
The men who actually produce the coal will have to be taken into consideration. A great deal could be said about this matter, but I want the minister to explain it fully. Do auditors from the finance department check the financial statements of the coal company, or do they accept the statement of the company's auditor? Their balance sheet from time to time shows that they have an income of a million and a half or two millions a year through subventions. Originally the subvention was intended to assist them to pay wages. They charge their wage bill 100 per cent to the cost of production, and I have never seen it shown where they received anything to assist in paying wages. When these subventions are paid there should be more examination into how they are handled. They 
should not be given to someone who can treat them as income and be able to write off a lot of depreciation and carry on other manipulation of accounts. There should be a full examination of the position of those who are producing coal in order that we may have some benefit from the money being spent this year in this way.

I know of no arrangement
between the dominion government and the Dominion Coal company by which the government guarantees standard profits or a subvention of fifteen cents, whichever is the larger. I have been connected with the coal business for only a matter of two or three months. There may be such a subsidy outstanding, but I doubt if there is. The subsidy to which I referred is based on one thing, namely, the increased cost of water transportation. Limestone must be transported from Wabana, and there is an increased cost in moving Brazilian ore from Brazil to Dosco. There is also an increased cost in the movement up the St. Lawrence. These are assessed against the costs of the base period, and the government pays the difference. I can assure my hon. friend that if it did not, there would be no steel produced in the Sydney area at the moment. It is necessary to do this in order to keep the industry alive. This happens to be the one steel industry where the war has made a real impact on transportation costs. We are making up the difference and thereby keeping the industry in production.

Is the
government storing sugar in Calgary?

The Department of Munitions and Supply does not deal in sugar. That question would have to be asked of the Department of Finance, which have the wartime prices and trade board under their jurisdiction.
Would the minister secure space from the Royal Canadian Air Force to provide storage for sugar?

We have nothing to do with
sugar.	.

You do
not even supply storage for it?

The tonnage being moved on our railroads in this war is ten times what it was in the last war. In the last war Mr. McAdoo took over the railroads of the United States and administered them for the remainder of the war. What is this government going to do? This government has been spending not millions but billions on the transportation systems of this country. We have appointed

War Appropriation-Supplies
a railway commission to run them in peace and war. Look at the Railway Act which provides for a board of transport commissioners to act for the people of this country. This 'board has fallen down.
In the United States during the last war the government of the day under Woodrow Wilson took over and administered the railroads on account of the congested condition of passenger and freight traffic. What is the policy of this government regarding the congestion on our railroads, all these boxcars we see along the right of way? We are not getting a total effort. The government is taxing the people of this country five billion dollars, and 30 per cent of it is not being used for war at all. All this storage that is taking place on the railway systems is being wasted. Some of the equipment is obsolete three months after it is furnished. The two transportation systems have fallen down on land, sea and in the air. Who is the minister responsible for it? The country wants to know, because the people are being taxed.
I think we should have some considered statement, not only from the Minister of Munitions and Supply but from other ministers. He is not to blame for this. We should hear from the Minister of Transport (Mr. Michaud), the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) and other ministers. In view of what the taxpayers are paying for this war, there should be some statement made. If the railway systems have fallen down and the enemy is at our gate, it is the duty of the government to take over the railroads for the benefit of the people and in order to have a total war effort. There should be no more of these boxcars all along the right of way. Look at the way in which the soldiers are treated. They cannot get accommodation on the trains, and then we have the fifty-mile bus rule. The people are sick and tired of it. The House of Commons might as well not meet at all if we have no control over the transportation system of this country.

It would not be fair to allow the statement of the hon. member for Broadview to go unchallenged. He knows, as does everyone, that since the beginning of the war the two great transportation systems of the country have not fallen down. On the contrary, they have met the needs of the country most magnificently in spite of the difficulty of replacing rolling stock and getting sufficient labour. Transportation on land within the country is under the control of the transport commissioners to the extent to which
the law gives them power to control. Then to take care of essential war services we have another control.
Why do you need the transit control and the board of transport commissioners?
The board of transport commissioners have duties and powers assigned to them under the Railway Act.
Why could these additional duties not have been assigned to the board of transport commissioners?

It would have meant adding personnel to the board. We decided to set up a special structure to take care of the essential war needs. This system is working out quite satisfactorily. The accumulation of war materials along the tracks referred to by the hon. member is not owing to lack of facilities to transport them to destination; it is because this is the most convenient place to store the goods until the consignees make requisition and ask that they be sent to the seaboard.
The railways have never fallen down in the transport of war material. They have provided the people who have purchased and paid for that material with storage along the lines, and whenever there is a requisition for a shipment the railways move the material to destination. There has been no hold-up, no delay whatever since the beginning of the war. The material along the lines is well taken care of. The owners are helping in the checking and protecting of the material, and it is done at their request and to meet the conditions which we have to face. As has already been said, Canada has been asked to accumulate war material, for obvious reasons, and the places where it is stored have been found by those who were directly interested to be the most convenient places for the purpose. Nobody is complaining about it-neither the owners of the goods, the manufacturers, nor those who are charged with the responsibility of transporting them. So that it is not fair to give the people of this country the impression that the transportation system of Canada has failed in its task during this war.

I do not wish to be critical of the present Minister of Transport, an hon. gentleman who I know is trying to do his duty. But I have seen evidences of the money which the Canadian National is spending on the United States portion of its system, and I know something about the comparative luxuriousness of the trains belonging to this road
War Appropriation-Supplies

upon which American soldiers are travelling in the United States. By contrast, last Friday I saw some of the Noah's Arks which were moving in and out of Camp Borden. Our great ally on the other side of the border would not stand for the kind of cattle trains-I call them that because that is what they are, just convertible cars which were formerly used for the transportation of various kinds of freight-which apparently are supposed to be good enough for our men. I have known the minister for many years; he is a kind-hearted man, and I hold him in respect; but I want to point out that ours is a citizens' army, composed of Canadians born in Canada, of many nationalities, and it is the view of a good many hon. members on both side of this chamber that these men are not being properly treated. During the war we are not interested in politics; our duty is to those who serve in the forces. I have talked to many men and have seen the kind of accommodation which the railways provide for them. The cars I saw last Friday going out of Camp Borden were not fit for human occupancy. I demand, in all courtesy, that we realize what our citizens' army is putting up with in return for a daily allowance of $1.30 plus fifty cents. After this war there will be a show-down with the two railway systems of this country. If they do not do their duty the government should take over the systems and administer them for the benefit of the people. We have spent a fortune on them and we are not getting adequate service. Look at the transportation of members of parliament out of this city and back. Look at the scenes at the Union station at Ottawa every night. Last evening when the empire parliamentary delegation arrived, one train was going out and one coming in, and if a car had jumped the track many people would have been killed. We have no explanation of such things. What is the railway commission doing? Are we to sit here as a lot of dummies and yes-men and nodders and approve the way in which the men in our armed forces are treated by the railways? I say, no; it is our duty to protest.

Another criticism which has been made does not seem to me to be fair. Facilities for passenger traffic,, as we all know, have been taxed to the limit ever since the war began. As regards transportation of the army, none of our soldiers are transported on United States lines; they all travel on Canadian lines, either Canadian Pacific or Canadian National. We all know that our rolling stock is used to capacity and that we cannot manufacture and get out of

the shops and factories the renewals and replacements of rolling stock as fast as the two systems would like to have them. There are priorities on locomotives, then on freight cars, and then on railway passenger cars. We have been unable to secure deliveries of orders placed in 1941. Our 1942 programme of over $25 millions for renewals of cars and locomotives has not yet been touched. Neither in the United States nor in Canada can we find factories capable of delivering the rolling stock as fast as we should like to have it. For that reason we have to be satisfied with what is available. I adimit that it is necessary to put up with some inconveniences, but conditions are such that we have to serve first the more pressing needs, and then wait until there is a de-congestion of the most needed requirements to turn our shops to the manufacturing of locomotives and passenger cars. Until that stage is reached, it will be impossible to find any better solution than the one we now have to be content with.

I suggest that the head
offices of the National system be transferred to Toronto as Ontario is its best customer.

They make all their money in the province of Ontario, anyway. Then we might get some results. Let the minister get rid of some of the deadwood in the Canadian National and engage some soldiers who know something about railways; it would be far better for the country.

Item agreed to.
7.	Loans to commodity companies, $15,000,000.

Under this item I should like to pursue a little further the discussion which arose a moment or so ago in respect of subsidies to the coal mining industry. The minister has said that he has not a great deal of experience with regard to coal; that is, not longer than during the past two or three months. I might suggest to him that the subventions which are paid on ooal-and perhaps the same would apply to steel to which he referred-are not paid to the coal companies, but specifically for the transportation of coal, and these subventions usually find their -way into the hands of transportation companies such as the railroads.
I do not know what is involved in the item "loans to commodity companies." There is a wide range of subjects embodied in each of these. We pass $100,000,000 here in a few minutes, and that must cover an extensive field. Surely we do not spend $100,000,000 on

War Appropriation-Supplies
pins; we must spend it on more than one commodity. However, with regard to loans to commodity companies, the government have been spending, for commodity companies, a certain amount on capital equipment which has expanded the companies. The government claim that they still own this capital equipment and that at the end of the war it will be returned to them, provided, of course, it is not worn out. It means anyway that the company itself has been expanded in its productive capacity, and expanded by the money which has been provided through war loans and so on. I ask the minister whether any money at all has been paid to coal mining companies for capital equipment in order to facilitate the production of more coal. Let me elucidate a little further in regard to the money that has been spent in connection with subventions to coal companies.
Two terms have been used in the last little while-subventions and subsidies. I do not know whether they are interchangeable. I do not think they are, because I believe that, in the truest sense of the word, subventions as applied to coal companies are payments for the movement of coal, while, in the true sense, subsidies may be given to coal mining companies.. I doubt whether any subsidies have been given to coal mining companies. Perhaps they have; I may not have the whole picture or be well enough informed on that. I know,, however, that year in and year out this house votes subventions for the movement of coal, and because that vote is not statutory, because it comes up every year, it could be dropped any year, and that means, of course, that coal mining companies will not expand their capital equipment. They will not say, "We will open up another mine here or sink another shaft there; there is good coal here and we will expand our capital equipment to develop it." The reason why they do not take that attitude is that after putting a good bit of money into such expansion of capital equipment, they may find the next year that the subsidy is reduced. They take a chance if they do that, and the result is that they will not do it.	,
A few weeks ago the Prime Minister announced a national emergency on account of a shortage of fuel. If there is an emergency by reason of a shortage of fuel, then in all probability we are in danger of our war production slowing up. There is now a serious situation of a huge coal strike in the United States. If our coal production should be reduced materially, it would not take very much to stop, perhaps almost overnight, the largest part of our production of munitions.
I do not know whether the minister is alarmed at that situation, but I shohld like to
know from him whether his department have done anything or contemplates doing anything toward the expansion of the coal mining industry of Canada in order to produce more Canadian coal for the Canadian production of munitions. The Minister of Labour is not at the moment in his seat to come to the minister's aid to-night. Someone will telephone him and he will come here in a couple of minutes. However, I should like to know whether the Minister of Munitions is entirely dependent upon the genius, if there is such a thing, in the labour department to see that the coal mining industry is not slowed up; for if it is, it will create a serious situation in Canada in the production of munitions.
Would the minister care to make a statement along that line? There are two points I am putting to him. First, is he dependent upon the Minister of Labour to see that the coal mining industry is kept continuously up to the fullest productive capacity, and, second, has he subsidized, or does he contemplate subsidizing that industry for the purpose of expanding coal production?

I should explain that this
item covers loans to commodity companies. As hon. members know, the government has from time to time accumulated large stocks of commodities, such as rubber, silk, wool, kapok and certain strategic metals. These are held by government-owned companies of the type called commodity companies, and the item in question covers the funds required by these companies to maintain stocks of strategic materials. My hon. friend was discussing the item we have just passed, namely, subsidies to coal companies. There is a difference between a subsidy and a subvention, as the terms are being used to-day. As the hon. member has said, a subvention is a sum of money paid to the transportation company to reduce the cost of transportation of coal, and therefore to enlarge the area which can be served from a coal-producing unit. Subsidies have been given for the purpose of increasing production. If it can be shown that by expending a certain sum of money more coal can be obtained from an operation, if equipment is required in a strip operation to step up production therefrom, these funds are advanced on terms that seem to be reasonable after a study of the individual case.
Under present conditions I would not hesitate to make any expenditure that promised any considerable increase in the production of coal. My hon. friend asks whether I am alarmed about the situation. I am alarmed about it, and I have said so in the house many times. Canada is a deficit country as
War Appropriation-Supplies

far as coal is concerned, and the deficit has reached extreme proportions. Naturally, with perhaps fifty per cent or more of our entire consumption of coal dependent upon sources over which we have no control, we are in an unpleasant position with trouble brewing in the coal fields on which we depend. He asks whether I am dependent on the Minister of Labour for stepping up coal production in Canadian mines. I do all I can to step up production within the jurisdiction of my portfolio, and the Minister of Labour does all he can in the administration of his portfolio to the same end. Naturally we work in close cooperation. I know of no operation which can be stepped up and which is not being stepped up by reason of lack of funds. If my hon. friend knows of such an operation, I would be very glad to be informed. One of our experts would go there immediately, and I can assure my hon. friend that if we were convinced that the output could be stepped up, the necessary funds would be forthcoming.
Mr. HAN'SELL:	What would be the procedure? The minister has made quite a liberal statement which will go out to the country. If a coal mining company says: "If we can get another fifty men we will put in another shaft, 'but we are not going to do it out of our own funds," what procedure would it have to adopt to get assistance? The coal mining industry of Canada over a period of years has been running pretty close to the edge, and a few cents reduction in the price of coal might mean putting them out of business. Would the coal miming company have to get in touch with the minister, or what?

The procedure would be for the secretary of the company to write to the secretary of the emergency ooal production board, with headquarters in Ottawa, and1 state the position. The board would immediately delegate one of its experts to go and examine the situation on the ground, and if the expert reported favourably the board would take action immediately.
May I ask what has happened to Allied Brass? Is it still under the same management?
Yes, it is turning out brass to capacity and has been, I think, since the present management took charge.

When the hon. member for
Macleod was speaking a moment ago, he made a statement which I think the minister

overlooked, and which may confuse those reading Hansard in the future. He stated that no subvention is ever paid directly to a coal company. That statement is not correct. At the present time the water-borne coal coming up the St. Lawrence is subsidized to the extent of one dollar a ton. The Dominion Coal company own the boats that bring that coal, the shipping company being a subsidiary of the coal company. In that way the subvention is paid. directly to the coal company. So that subventions do go direct to the coal companies in some cases.
Mr. MiaoNICOL: The minister said yesterday that I might bring up the question of magnesium metal on this item.
Yes.

The minister a year ago gave us a glowing account of what he hoped at that time to achieve from the plant that was proposed to be erected. He stated that the market price on May 20, 1942, of magnesium metal was between 33 and 34 cents a pound. Then he aded, "We expect to get it for about half that, but I would not care to be too specific about it." Well, this new plant was put in at a cost of $4469,500, of which $820,000 was working capital, according to a return which was brought down some days ago, but instead of getting magnesium metal from this plant at half the price of 33 or 34 cents a pound, or 16 to 17 cents a pound, we are paying, according to the return that was brought down on May 24 of this year, 39-7 cents a pound. AVould the minister explain why the price of magnesium metal is so high?
I remember when I brought up the subject of magnesium metal in 1941-this was before it came into the minister's department-I asked the Minister of Mines and Resources a question arising out of an article which had appeared in the paper about a magnesium plant. My question was about magnesium metal, but the Minister of Mines and Resources in his reply spoke of magnesium-two different things, entirely. Magnesium is an explosive; magnesium metal is a metal. The Minister of Mines and Resources said at that time that a plant was being erected- up the Gatineau to produce magnesium. Later on the plant to produce magnesium metal, the plant likely referred to in the article, was erected at Haley. At that time I was interested in the question of magnesium metal, because I knew a man in Hamilton-I have known him for quite a few years-a man by the name of Ralph Keemle, a regular genius who had developed a process for the production of

War Appropriation-Supplies
magnesium metal from dolomite through the use of electricity, and I was informed that he could produce magnesium metal at from 8 to 10 cents a pound, which is from one-fifth to one-quarter of the price we are now paying. I think the minister said that Mr. Keemle had been consulted, or had been invited to Ottawa, but if he was invited to Ottawa he got rather short shift, because the government, as everyone knows, took up the process that had been developed by our own national research, and brought about the formation of a crown company. I never did think that Mr. Keemle got a square deal or was treated fairly. I always felt that anyone who was capable of developing a process that worked, as he did, should be given a chance. But that is all past now. What I am anxious to know now is why the price of magnesium metal is so high? Why is it so much higher than the minister informed the house it would be when this new plant got into operation? I should also like to ask him how many pounds of magnesium metal are used in the average aeroplane? The return that was brought down on May 24 of this year showed that we have produced up to the end of April, 1943, 1,186 tons of magnesium metal, and if the amount which was reported on a former occasion as the approximate amount which was used per .plane, or 2000 pounds, that would mean that we have produced up to the end of April this year enough for more than 500 planes.
What in the world are we to do with this plant after the war? Magnesium metal is a light metal, two-thirds the weight of aluminum, but it cannot take the place of aluminum in every respect. Aluminum has to be used as an alloy to prevent an explosion of magnesium metal, and this latter metal is used as an alloy in aluminum to give rigidity. It is quite an investment we have made in this plant. I have no fault to find with the plant having been built. On the contrary I am inclined to congratulate the minister for having the plant put up to produce magnesium metal. But why is the metal so costly, so much higher than the minister thought would be the price when the plant was in operation?

My hon. friend will appreciate that the government embarked on a new process for the manufacture of magnesium metal. The process was moved from a small pilot plant into large scale production. Certain tests were made as a result of studies of the results from the pilot plant, from which certain assumptions were made as to the cost of large-scale operation. I am optimistic enough to
think that those predictions were not so far out of line as the costs during the month of April, which my hon. friend has given, would indicate. There has been some difficulty in the metallurgy of the retorts; there has been a great deal of distortion and breaking there, which has been a source of considerable cost in the matter of supplies. The cost of quarrying, milling and reduction has not yet been brought down to a reasonable level. As my hon. friend knows, we have opened up a new quarry, and we have not really got the quarrying costs shaken down. The other large item is the cost of ferro-silicate, which is mixed with the powdered rock to make briquettes. The cost of that operation is considerably higher than had beeen anticipated, owing to the war situation. I would point out, however, that the capital expenditure for this plant has been very low as compared to alternative processes. We investigated the cost of a chemical process for producing ten tons of magnesium a day, and the estimated cost given us was something over $9,000,000. This plant has been built for a little over $3,000,000; it is producing to capacity, and I am optimistic enough to hope that the price will be brought down to a competitive level with the chemical process.
Then my hon. friend asked about the future of magnesium after the war. At the present time this plant is supplying all Canada's needs for magnesium metal, with a fair surplus left over for export. Magnesium is a metal that is much stronger than aluminum pound for pound; it has that advantage over aluminum. The disadvantage is that magnesium is subject to corrosion, whereas aluminum is not. The two are competitive in the light metal field for certain uses, particularly in the building of aeroplanes and aeroplane engines; in many uses magnesium is essential and has great advantages over aluminum. Undoubtedly there will be a market, and a considerable market, for magnesium metal after the war. Whether Canada can have a share of that market will depend upon whether our costs can be brought down so that they will be competitive with other types of production. In any event, Canada has an assured supply of magnesium for the war and for the post-war period.

Has Canada tried to obtain magnesium from salt water, as they are doing in Britain? [DOT]
Mr. HOWE; The extraction of magnesium from salt water is a well known processs; it is used in the United States and in Britain. It is the old chemical process. Canada went to a thermal process, which we believe to be the
War Appropriation-Supplies

process of the future and which involves a very much smaller capital expenditure. But, as I say, I have not been able to bring the cost of production down to the cost which I was once optimistic enough to give the house.

Last year serious shortages developed in some of the base metals such as zinc, lead, copper and several others. As a result of that shortage, the government entered upon a policy of stimulating the production of certain metals through the agency of a crown company known as Wartime Metals corporation. Apparently that corporation has taken over the operation of certain mines; a return brought down in the house on March 24 listed twelve that had been so taken over. What progress has been made in stimulating the production of base metals, and what is the policy of the government in regard to supplying miners for base metal mines? In British Columbia, mines operated by private companies are under a handicap as compared with those which have been taken over by Wartime Metals corporation. I understand that priority for labour is given to the mines operated by the crown company; yet in at least some cases production could be increased more rapidly by sending ten men, let us say, to a mine operated by a private company than by sending the same ten men to a mine operated by the crown company. I think the government would be well advised to revise its present policy and at least give a private company with an operating mine equal priority in labour with the mine operated by the crown.
Then I should like to know from the minister whether any loans have been made to private companies; whether consideration has been given to extending the policy by loaning money to operating companies. Again it might be that if this were done it would result in greater production, and getting that production more quickly, than by putting the same amount of money into a mine operated by the crown. Would the minister explain what the policy is with regard to these mines?

My hon. friend will understand that Canada has not been short of the metals he mentions. Canada is the largest exporter of metals in the world, but there has been a world shortage of copper, lead, nickel and zinc, and Canada has succeeded in helping to meet those shortages to a considerable extent. This indicates that the efforts of the government to increase the production of metals of which there is a world shortage for war purposes have met with a good deal of success. Wartime Metals corporation has been the instrument of the government in certain operations, more particularly in the field of rare metals such as chrome, tungsten, molybdenum and metals of that kind, of which Canada has not sufficient. The company has been quite successful. It has brought in a chrome mine in the eastern townships; it is operating what we believe to be the richest tungsten mine on the continent, which we hope will make Canada self-contained in regard to tungsten.
Mr. GREEN Which mine is that?
It is out in British Columbia.
The Emerald mine?

Yes, I believe so. It is actually carrying on certain developments for the production of strategic minerals. These are developments which private industry has not been willing to undertake, owing to the fact that the use of these strategic minerals in peace time is so small that no peace-time future for the mines could be assured, sufficient to permit private enterprise to finance.
The hon. member has asked if the government has financed the development of mines. The Canadian government has not done so. I am not sure I can say it has never done so, but it has not been the practice because the Canadian government has not been short of standard base metals. But it has arranged with the Metals Reserve Corporation of the United States to finance certain properties, the output of which would be helpful to the metals situation in the United States.
That is all under the direction of the metals controller in Canada.

That is correct. We have encouraged any production that would be helpful to the war effort, and we have arranged for financing by the Metals Reserve corporation of properties which promised to be immediately helpful to the war effort. I know of no proposal that had real merit and which promised quick results which has not had help extended to it, through the agency of the metals controller or by Wartime Metals corporation.

Does the government operate these mines through Wartime Metals Corporation, or in some cases is money loaned to a private company, and operations carried on by that private company?

Yes.

I should like to refer to the question of the expropriation of property carried out by the department, or by an administrative body within the department. Has each government department machinery to handle the expropriation of land or other property, or is there one body within the government which handles that particular aspect of government enterprise?

The Department of Munitions and Supply has retained the land department of the Canadian National Railways to handle the expropriation and acquisition of property required by the department, either for airports or for industrial purposes. The other departments either have their own officials, or use some other agency of government.

I was particularly interested in learning whether any uniformity of policy as between the departments exists? Ordinarily when an expropriation takes place the individual concerned is compensated to a higher degree than would normally obtain if the property were sold on the open market. In most instances property is taken which the individual may not be desirous of selling. I
have in mind a case where an individual purchased a parcel of land for $150, and had paid $50 taxes. He considers the property worth every cent put into it, but the departmental officials assert that $10 is a fair price for it, in their expropriation proceedings.
In certain departments we have found no such condition. In fact one sometimes thinks they are generous to the extreme. In a matter of this kind we ought to have facilities for preventing the development of any unfair situation. What final say does the individual have, if he wishes to protest against any expropriation? Must he abide by the decision of the department?

No, not at all. Once expropriation is taken, the matter goes before the Exchequer Court of Canada, The owner need not accept any offer made by the department, and the department is not bound to make an offer to the owner. Expropriation involves adjudication by the exchequer court. To save litigation, an attempt is usually made to settle with the owner without going to court. In small purchases an expert for the department makes up his mind as to what he believes to be a fair value for the land, and makes an offer to the owner. If the owner, the officer and the department agree, the matter can be settled without going to court. But no property owner need necessarily accept any offer made by the department; he can let the exchequer court make the decision.

When we were debating the munitions and supply bill I raised the matter of better representation of labour in the Department of Munitions and Supply. I should like the minister to comment upon the possibilities of that. The Department of Munitions and Supply is a specialized department which covers a multitude of matters, but it does seem to me that there is one serious lack, namely, representation of labour in- the so-called munitions and supply empire. What is the reason for this? What steps has the minister in mind to cure the situation?

As my hon. friend knows,
the predecessor of the Department of Munitions and Supply was the war supply board. This was made up of four men, one of whom was a representative of labour in the person of Mr. Howard Chase, the highest ranking member of the railway brotherhoods in Canada, a man of exceptional ability. When the department was formed Mr. Chase was made director-general of labour relations. I believe he performed excellent service for labour and for the department. His work was outstanding, but inside of twelve months the one desire of organized labour in Canada was that Mr. Chase should be severed from the Department of Munitions and Supply. The only time I have known the Canadian congress of labour and the trades labour council to be unanimous was when they pointed out quite vigorously that it was the duty of the Department of Labour to attend to all labour matters and that the Department of Munitions and Supply should not have a director-general of labour relations. The position was abolished at about the time the national war labour board was formed, and this board took over the functions which were being performed by Mr. Chase. We certainly had the approval of organized labour generally in that step.

We have appointed representatives of labour to operating boards. There are very few operating boards, such as Wartime Housing, Toronto Shipbuilding and so on that do not have representatives of labour. Almost any operating board that my hon. friend can name I am sure will have a representative of labour. These men have been most helpful to the different projects. I would certainly add a labour man to any operating board that might be appointed in the future. If there are any difficulties in my department through not having labour representation, I am very much surprised to hear it.

The minister has been told about the housing situation in Toronto. I notice that under the new scheme of converting larger houses into apartments about $250,000 will be expended in Toronto to convert fifty houses. When they asked for applications for conversion I understand they got over a thousand. The conversion of fifty houses in Toronto will not do very much good. A great deal has been done to provide war-time housing in other cities, but no housing of this type has been provided in Toronto.
The minister states that workers can find places to go in Toronto, that there is no lack of accommodation. The fact is that people are being crowded. As I said before, families of four are crowding into one or two rooms in the slum districts, because that is the only place they can go. Unless some relief is given, I do not know what will happen. Some of these districts will be converted into slums. The minister said that there would be an exodus of people from Toronto as time went on. because not so much work would be done in the city. He must remember that there are many industries in the small communities around Toronto, and there is an exodus of workers out, of the city every morning and back again at night. In some cases the beds are never allowed to get cold; one man gets up to go to work and another man goes to bed. I wish the minister would give some consideration to Toronto in this connection.
Is the administration of this conversion plan to be under Wartime Housing or under National Housing?
