There are a few remarks I wish to make with reference to civil aviation and also post-war civil aviation and its relationship to the development of northern Canada. First of all, I wish to congratulate the minister upon recently informing us of the opening up of the transatlantic airline service. I know he mentioned then that it was not for commercial purposes, but I do hope it is the beginning of a post-war civil aviation programme. In the meantime, however, it will greatly facilitate the carriage of mail for the overseas forces. During the last few years we have had very important construction development in northern Canada, undertaken largely by the United States forces for the purpose of supporting United States operations in the Aleutians and Alaska, or to assist in the ferrying of aircraft to Alaska. The project that has received the most notice is, of course, the Alaska highway, which has been constructed and is now in operation. However, there are many other projects of equal importance. For instance, there is the development of the oil fields in the Fort Norman area and the survey of a railroad from Prince George to Fairbanks.
I note by press reports of the last few days that the United States army has done a great deal of development work in the Fort Norman oil fields. I feel sure that it will be of great assistance to Canada, not only now but after the war when we open up this territory as we all hope and expect we shall. These developments have stirred the imagination of Canadians, and the question is being asked, why not develop these resources, and also, what is Canada prepared to do when the war is over?
At this point I should like to pay a tribute to one of the pioneers of civilian aviation, Don Martin of Montreal, whose untimely passing
War Appropriation-Supplies

from among us a few days ago removes one of those pioneers with great vision of aviation. He will be greatly missed by the old-line bush pilots and bush operating companies, for whom he has done so much in the help he gave them in building up bush routes in northern Canada.
We in Canada have entered into an agreement with the United States government whereby all immovable facilities constructed by the United States in Canada will revert to this country at the end of the war or within a specified time thereafter. If we are to carry on the development of our northern areas when the United States forces withdraw, a definite programme of post-war development should be planned now. The present flying operations in northern Canada have been essentially a war-time undertaking. However, this flying is really airline flying with modern heavy transport aircraft and with radio aids to navigation that are found on Trans-Canada air liners. It goes without saying that at the end of the war the vast majority of the wartime projects in northern Canada will be discontinued, and the necessity for the present transport operations in that area will cease. The continuance of post-war flying in northern areas with the exception of bush operations is dependent on active economic development there. Therefore, I ask, is Canada making adequate and proper preparations to develop our arctic regions? The economic development of Canada up to date has largely been confined to the southern part of our country. However, it is now being realized that the northern regions have tremendous resources which are capable of development.
That very important and profitable development of these resources is not only feasible but practicable has been amply demonstrated by the Russians, who for a good many years past have had an active programme of exploration and exploitation in Siberia. To-day, with the help of the present advances in aviation, Canada's north assumes ever-increasing importance. Trans-polar flying, which is already a practical undertaking, awaits only a little further advance in long-distance stratosphere flying to make it a commercial possibility. In view of these events, the Canadian arctic regions can no longer be regarded as a wilderness but must be looked upon as a vital thoroughfare linking North America by air with Asia and the continent of Europe.
There are many reasons, then, to support the belief that Canada's post-war expansion will be northward toward the arctic. This expansion has been made possible by war-time advances in aviation, but its permanent basis

must rest on the economic development of the arctic regions. If this development is to be undertaken successfully and promptly as soon as the war is over, steps should be taken immediately to embark on a programme of investigation and exploration. Therefore I suggest that a strong interdepartmental committee of the government should be formed to explore all possible avenues of development. I understand that an international committee has already been formed to coordinate the economic development of northwestern Canada and Alaska; but we need more than that. We need a national committee to be responsible for the whole of northern Canada. Incidentally it might be observed that the United States government has already organized a very strong group to undertake similar investigations. This indicates that the United States is taking a great interest in the post-war international air routes which traverse northern Canada. We have many competent and experienced1 men available, men who pioneered northern Canada and the many bush flying routes working in cooperation with mining men, who through the use of aircraft developed our northern mining areas.
We also have to-day a great airline company, the C.P.A., who have taken over many of the bush-line companies and are operating a successful service in many parts of Canada.
What company is that?

I do not know whether my hon. friend has ridden on many of their planes, but I assume he has ridden on some of their trains and I hope he enjoyed the ride.
We have available in Canada men who are well acquainted with the north, but the knowledge and ability of these men must be focused collectively on specific problems and, further, their efforts must be correlated for the purpose of definite action under the strongest possible government support.
A few of the problems to which such a committee, if it is set up, should give consideration, are the following:
1.	The post-war development of Fort Norman oil fields and McMurray tar sands.
2.	Active exploration for new oil fields.
3.	The post-war disposition of the Alaska highway.
4.	The development of post-war air routes to Europe by Hudson bay, Greenland and Iceland; and to Europe and Asia via the northwest staging route and the Mackenzie river route.

War Appropriation-Supplies
5.	The investigation of trans-polar air routes to Europe and Asia, including the selection of suitable bases and plans for development.
6.	Meteorological investigations, particularly as they relate to trans-polar flying.
7.	Investigations of low-temperature flying, involving low temperature operation of engines and accessory equipment. The United States is already carrying out an extensive programme of research in this field.
8.	Investigation of problems connected with the construction of airfields on permanently frozen soils.
9.	The study of suitable types of buildings for arctic regions.
10.	Extension of the navigation season out of Churchill by the coordinated use of aircraft and powerful ice-breakers.
In addition, Mr. Chairman, I know, and I think the committee knows, that there are many other problems of tremendous importance to the people of Canada so far as the north and the development of aviation are concerned, which I believe go hand in hand together. I hope the government will take action now to see to it that we in Canada have our place in the aviation picture of the universe when this struggle is over.

I should like to say a
few words on this item, with particular reference to the subsection which deals with the operation and maintenance of municipal airports. I refer particularly to Stevenson field at Winnipeg. This is a matter of definite interest not only to the people of the part of the country from which I come; it is one of those cases where a local interest is also a national interest. Previous speakers already have emphasized the importance of Canada's future in the air and the necessity of our realizing the steps that should be taken to assure our position in the post-war world. Winnipeg, as is well-known, lies in the centre of the country on an east and west line, and practically in the centre of the continent of North America; and we feel that it is important to Canada's future in the air that we have in Winnipeg an adequate airport. By "adequate" I mean an airport with facilities that make it possible to take care of the largest planes now flying, or that may fly in the near future.
Perhaps the minister is aware that I have been endeavouring to get some information in connection with the attitude of the government toward Stevenson field by certain questions which I have placed on the order
paper. I may take a moment or two to summarize what I have done. First of all, on May 13 I gave notice of a motion asking for the tabling of documents relating to the possible enlargement of Stevenson field, but on May 17 the Minister of National Defence for Air advised me across the floor of the house that the material for which I was asking was quite voluminous and suggested that perhaps I would look at it privately and indicate what portions I should like to have brought down. Subsequently his department gave me the privilege of looking through that file. I found it very interesting; it dealt with many improvements to the field for which the government was responsible and which I was glad to note, but it did not make any reference to ways and means of lengthening the runways, which is the matter we feel should be given immediate attention, both for war-time needs and for the post-war period. After having looked over the file which I was shown by the Department of National Defence for Air, I placed a question on the order paper on May 18, in which I asked:
1.	Has any consideration been given by the government, or by any department or branch thereof, to the question of re-routing the Souris branch of the Canadian Pacific Railway in order to permit a northward extension of Stevenson field at Winnipeg?
2.	Have any representations in the above matter been made to the government, or to any department or branch thereof, and if so, by whom?
That question was passed as an order for return, and when the return was brought down the answer to question No. 1 was "no." The answer to question No. 2 was "yes," that representations had been made by the St. James-Winnipeg airport commission. Subsequently, on June 16, the house passed a motion in my name calling for the tabling of a copy of those representations, together with any replies made by the government. Of course that was only a few days ago, and the return has not been brought,down as yet.
The department of mines and natural resources of Manitoba is taking a keen interest in this matter and has prepared a folder which contains two quite interesting maps, one of North America by itself and the other showing North America in relation to the north pole and to Europe, Asia and Africa which lie on the other side of the north pole. This map indicates the strategic position held by Winnipeg, not only for Winnipeg but for Canada as a whole, in the air map of the world which as we now realize centres around the northern part of the globe. In addition to the efforts

War Appropriation-Supplies

being made by the department of mines and natural resources of Manitoba, one of the Winnipeg newspapers has been doing what I regard, in spite of its political opposition to the group to which I belong, as a commendable job in emphasizing the importance of the taking of action at the present time. The Winnipeg Tribune has pointed out that at Stevenson field we have the possibilities of an airport to serve the whole of Canada in the post-war world. It is located conveniently to the city, being only three miles from the centre of Winnipeg. As we all know, it is rather unusual on the North American continent to have airport facilities quite so close to the centre of a great city. Even before the government, under the stress of war, assumed a major share of the responsibility for the operation of the field, the airport had facilities which were quite modern; in fact it had everything but runways of sufficient length for the largest planes flying to-day. On May 15 of this year, in a feature article dealing with this matter, the Tribune said:
AH types of planes which so far have come here-big bombers included-have been able to land at Stevenson field, but it took skilful piloting to bring them down safely. On the present runways they could just make it, with little or nothing to spare.
A little later in the same article, after the assets of Stevenson field had been recounted, I find this further statement which I should like to quote:
But its runways are not long enough. . . .
What is my hon. friend quoting from?

From the Winnipeg
Tribune of May 15, 1943.
Who was it said he could not land there, or just made it?

This is an article signed by Mr. L. F. Earl who said), if I may quote that part again, that all types of planes have been able to land at Stevenson field but that it took skilful piloting to bring them down safely.
I do not think it would require an exceptionally skilful pilot to land at that field.

The article goes on to say:
A modern aerodrome, so sa3' the engineers, should have minimum runways of 4,000 feet and should be capable of expansion to 5,000

feet. This is on a sea level basis. Winnipeg is about 800 feet above sea level, so these distances should be extended to 4,200 and 5,300 feet respectively.
The point at issue at the present time, in view of the fact that our longest runway is only 4,400 feet, is the necessity, if these runways are to be lengthened', of re-routing a portion of the Souris branch of the Canadian Pacific railway which runs just north of the present limit of Stevenson field. At the present time there is a good deal of vacant land there, and the railway could be shifted to make possible the lengthening of these' runways. The newspaper to which I have already referred has been dealing with this matter at some length. It has carried reports from Ottawa to the effect that no consideration is being given to this matter as yet, and it expresses apprehension lest the matter be put off too long, and something happen to that vacant land north of Stevenson field, with the result that in order to have longer runways it might be necessary to go farther out into the country, or that Winnipeg might be by-passed altogether.
Despite the fact that the answer in the return which I have already mentioned was "no", would the minister state whether any consideration has been given to the shifting of the railway line to which I have referred, to make possible the northward1 extension of that field, and the subsequent lengthening of the runway?
I should also like to ask-and I confess I do so on the basis of rumours I have heard; I cannot substantiate them, but they are disquieting-whether anj; plans are being made for establishing in Manitoba an airport at some point other than Stevenson field, where such a fine start has been made. Would the minister authoritatively set aside that rumour, and let us know that any future enlargement of airport facilities will be at the field where, as I say, considerable progress has already been made and where facilities are in close proximity to the centre of a great city which, as I have pointed out, is situated in the centre of the continent, and is in a location strategic to the future of air travel in Canada?
I should hope the minister would reply to my question as to whether any consideration is being given to the measures necessary to lengthen these runways, and whether in

War Appropriation-Air Services
his knowledge plans are under way for any other airport in Manitoba to take the place of Stevenson field.

Stevenson field is a first class airport, by any standards. It is used by Trans-Canada Air Lines, by the ferrying service, and by the Royal Canadian Air Force. It is quite satisfactory for any use to which it is being put at the moment. The approaches are ideal. There is much more to an airport than the length of its runways. There are many airports with longer runways than those on Stevenson field which are not nearly so good as Stevenson field. The services using the field to-day are satisfied with the present conditions, and it is a very busy airport.
Recently the city has interested itself in exploring the possibilities of extending the runways. The department has given the city certain advice in that matter. A plan was sent out about a week or ten days ago, containing the department's suggestion for any future expansion of the airport. May I point out that the airport is not the property of the dominion government, but rather that of the municipality of St. James. The department is the lessee of the airport only for war purposes. If during the war the need for a larger airport presents itself, that need will be met by the dominion government. After the war the airport will be turned back to its owner, and the government will at any time discuss with the owner the possibility of enlargements.
Will the minister answer my other question? Are there any plans for replacing Stevenson field with any other airport so far as Manitoba is concerned?
No.
Item agreed to.

As I shall not be able to read this in ten minutes I shall leave it for another time. The hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) asked if the publication Wings pays for itself. It does not. The monthly revenue more than covers the purchase of materials and the typesetting that is done by a civilian firm. In effect, the only public expense is for salaries of service personnel and for the shipping of the paper to the stations. It is still a new venture and has every right to expect that, as it develops, expenditures will be reduced. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle asked about the cost of publishing Wings. The total cost is $1,487 a month. The revenue for the first three months was $540 a month. The monthly deficit is $947 at the present time. The cost is made up of $346 for materials; $112 for typesetting; $265 for shipping; and $764 for editorial staff; or a total of $1,487.
The hon. member for St. John-Albert (Mr. Hazen) asked if buses are attached to the
Pennfield Ridge station to take personnel to the city. Buses are not attached to this station to take personnel to the city. Saint John is thirty-nine miles from the station, and a civilian bus service is in operation. He asked also if orders have been issued to restrict the use of staff cars. The answer is, yes. The King's Regulations and Orders for the Royal Canadian Air Force, Canadian air publication No. 23, gives specific instructions with regard to restricting the use of staff cars. Orders are issued periodically with regard to this procedure.
The hon. member for Prince Edward-Lennox (Mr. Tustin) inquired about the cost of posters. One hundred and fifty thousand posters, size twenty-five by thirty-eight inches, were produced at a cost of $25,302, or, roughly, seventeen cents each. Twenty thousand posters in French were produced at a cost of $6,000. Fifty thousand posters in connection with recruiting for the women's division were produced at a cost of $6,900, or, roughly, fourteen cents each.
The hon. member for Peterborough West (Mr. Fraser) asked whether helicopters can land on water. They can be fitted with flotation bags which will permit them to be so landed.
The hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson) asked if the Jacobs engine has been satisfactory. Since the original teething troubles were overcome, the Jacobs engine has given good satisfaction. A recent survey has shown that accidents on account of engine failure in aircraft fitted with Jacobs engines occur at a rate of only one in about twenty-nine thousand hours of flying, a rate which compares favourably with other engines. I think these are all the questions I can answer before eleven o'clock.
Progress reported.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
